Release builds stay hardened: Go -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w", Flutter web --no-source-maps.
data.shared-ui-components#Shared UI component: Pages that more than one Runink app shows come from org-runink/ui: design tokens and transport (foundation), billing, datasources, profile, access, voice, comms, and judgement. PULSE mounts the Go handler with its own hooks and depends on the Flutter package by path. To try an unmerged ui branch, use a private GOWORK and a gitignored flutter/pubspec_overrides.yaml.
data.the-apps-backend-address#The app\u0026rs:
The Flutter client reads PULSE_BACKEND_URL from a --dart-define. It is resolved in this order:
the --dart-define, baked in at compile time; on web, config.json next to the bundle ({"backendUrl": …}), which a deployment can change without rebuilding; on web, the origin the page was served from; on native, http://localhost:50051. A deployment normally leaves the define empty and serves the web build from the backend itself (PULSE_WEB_DIR), so the app and its gRPC-Web API are same-origin: no CORS entry and no per-deployment URL.
data.the-backend-image#The backend image: grpc/Dockerfile builds the image from the repository root. Its base images come through the BASE_REGISTRY and FLUTTER_SDK_REGISTRY build arguments, each pinned by digest. See Image build arguments.

data: PULSE’s API is gRPC, package pulse.v1, plus the shared runink.ui.*.v1 services. There is no REST or JSON API for business data.
data.a2a-calling-pulse-from-another-agent#A2A:
PULSE publishes itself as an Agent2Agent (A2A) agent for FACE and the Runink TIDE fleet:
Discovery: GET /.well-known/agent-card.json. Calls: JSON-RPC at /a2a, with a PULSE session as a bearer token in the Authorization header. Calls without a valid session are refused. Choose a persona with the message metadata key skill. The default is market-analyst.
Skill Persona market-analyst Diagnostics, SWOT, positioning content-creator Channel content copywriter Long-form content and whitepapers strategy-agent Prescriptive 30-day plans radar-agent Trend and profile research
data.authenticate#Authenticate:
Call IdentityService/Login with a username and password. The token is in accessToken:
TOK=$(grpcurl -plaintext -d '{"username":"admin","password":""}' \ localhost:52000 pulse.v1.IdentityService/Login | jq -r '.accessToken') Send it on every other call:
grpcurl -plaintext -H "authorization: Bearer $TOK" -d '{}' \ localhost:52000 pulse.v1.CampaignService/ListCampaigns Only three things work without a token: IdentityService/Login, ModelService/GetModelStatus, and reflection (when it is turned on).
Refresh a session at POST /auth/refresh. See HTTP endpoints.
data.browsers-the-session-cookie#Browsers: th:
A browser has nowhere safe to keep a token — anything the page can store, any script on the page can read — so the web client never receives one. It asks for cookie mode by sending x-pulse-session: cookie on Login or on POST /auth/google. The backend answers with no token in the body and sets the session as a host-only, HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookie, which the browser then attaches to every call by itself. Sign out at POST /auth/logout, which revokes the session and clears the cookie; page scripts cannot clear it themselves.
Because a cookie travels with any request to the host, whoever wrote the page, a call authenticated by the cookie must prove it came from the PULSE app, in two ways, both required:
the header x-pulse-csrf: 1 — a cross-site form cannot set a custom header; an Origin the server trusts: the server’s own host, PULSE_PUBLIC_BASE_URL, or an exact entry of CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS. A * never counts. Native clients are unaffected: a bearer header is not sent automatically, so it is not a cross-site risk, and neither proof is needed for it.
data.discover-the-schema#Discover the schema:
With PULSE_GRPC_REFLECTION=true on a local server:
grpcurl -plaintext localhost:52000 list grpcurl -plaintext localhost:52000 describe pulse.v1.LeadService Reflection is off by default and must stay off on deployed instances. Without it, use the .proto files in grpc/api/proto/pulse/v1/.
data.errors#Errors:
PULSE uses standard gRPC codes and puts a sentence meant for a person in the message. Common ones:
Code Typical cause Unauthenticated Missing, expired, or revoked token PermissionDenied Licence invalid, or your role does not allow the call FailedPrecondition Something must be set up first, for example a HubSpot connection or PULSE_APPLY_ENABLED InvalidArgument A required field is missing or has a bad value ResourceExhausted Rate limit, or the inference plane is at capacity Unavailable A dependency failed: HubSpot, GA4, speech synthesis, media storage Unimplemented The feature does not exist in this deployment, for example still-image generation NotFound No such record, or it belongs to another account Aborted A long run ended in failure; the stream closes with this and the run’s own error See Troubleshooting for specific messages.
data.roles#Roles: A valid session is the first gate; your account’s role is the second, read fresh from the server on every call rather than from the token. Reads that spend no model time and change nothing need viewer; anything that generates, writes, dials out or places a call needs editor; the access and messaging-settings methods need admin. A call above your role fails with PermissionDenied. GetCurrentUser and Logout work for any signed-in account, so someone with no role assigned can still see that and sign out.
data.streaming-calls#Streaming calls:
Every AI generator is a server-streaming RPC that returns stream StreamChunk:
Field Meaning text The next piece of output. May be empty. is_final True on the last chunk section A section marker, for example positioning, swot, or grounding progress 0.0 to 1.0 metadata Extra key-value data agent_tasks Actions the backend actually performed, such as a scrape. These are recorded facts, not model claims. A chunk with tasks may have no text. Long generations can go quiet while the model thinks. When a stream has been silent for a while, the server sends a status frame so proxies do not drop the connection and so you can tell waiting from stalled. A status frame has empty text and is_final false — append text blindly and you append nothing — and says what it is in metadata:
Metadata key Meaning keepalive 1 on a frame that exists to keep the stream open phase queued, generating, finishing, editing, refused, or at_capacity tokens Tokens produced so far in the current pass, approximate token_budget The ceiling this pass was dispatched with, not a prediction refused means a guardrail declined to release the output: a complete answer, and the next move is to change the brief rather than retry it. at_capacity means the inference plane is saturated, where retrying later is right.
Use a generous deadline: a long document can take tens of minutes on CPU.
When the model is busy and admission control is on, a call can fail with ResourceExhausted. Retry after a few minutes.
data.tie-runs-to-your-screen#Tie runs to your: Set x-agent-trace-id on your calls, and send the same value as session in ActivityService/SubscribeAgentActivity. Then the activity stream shows only the runs your client started. See Agent activity.
data.transports#Transports:
Everything is on one port.
Client How it connects Native gRPC (Go, grpcurl, the Linux and Android app) HTTP/2 with content-type: application/grpc Browsers gRPC-Web over the same port For browsers served from another origin, the origin must be listed in CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS. The allowed request headers include Authorization, X-Grpc-Web, grpc-timeout, x-agent-trace-id, x-idempotency-key, x-pulse-csrf, and x-pulse-session.

data:
Runink PULSE: Prescriptive Unified Lead & Social Engine does the weekly marketing work of a small business: it works out what to post, where and for whom, writes it, posts what you approve, answers simple comments if you let it, finds leads, and tells you what came of it.
Your first ten minutes are one check-up: PULSE reads your website, asks you a few plain questions, and fills the app with what it found. This page takes you from the sign-in screen to that first check-up. It assumes PULSE is already running for you; to run it on your own computer, see Run PULSE locally.
data.connect-your-accounts-when-you-are-ready:
A check-up needs no connected account. Connecting them is what turns “not measured” into real figures and lets PULSE post what you approve. Open Settings → Integrations. See Connect your accounts.
Nothing is posted until you approve it, and not even then while your administrator has publishing switched off. PULSE’s AI runs on your PULSE’s own model server, which serves everyone’s requests in turn, so a generation can take a few minutes. On the Lite plan, each seat’s first 10 tasks a day run at full speed; after that they keep running more slowly until midnight on the seat’s clock. See Plans.
data.next#Next: Signing in Brand Analysis How PULSE works
data.read-what-it-found#Read what it found:
When the check-up ends, Brand Analysis fills in. Start with the cards at the top: each one is a page with a one-line answer and a dot that says whether that answer was measured. Then read Needs you now: it lists the fixes in your plan, the drafts waiting for your approval and the replies waiting for you. See Brand Analysis.
The check-up also prepares work for you, and nothing of it goes out by itself:
Campaigns shows the campaign PULSE proposes, and the drafts it wrote, waiting for your approval. Leads shows the people the check-up found, in New, and your follow-up tasks under To do today.
data.sign-in#Sign in:
Open PULSE. Until you sign in, every page sends you to the sign-in screen. It offers Sign in with Google, a username and password, or both, depending on how your PULSE is set up. With a password, sign in with your username, not your email address. See Signing in.
PULSE opens on Brand Analysis.
data.start-your-first-check-up#Start your fir:
Before the first check-up, Brand Analysis says No check-up yet and what a check-up shows: your site score, whether AI answers and Google searches name you, and the leads and competitors PULSE finds.
Choose New site audit. The check-up asks one question per screen. Only the first one is required; every other screen has Skip.
What’s your website? PULSE opens that one page to read how the site describes itself and which social pages it links to. If the page cannot be opened, the next screen says so and the check-up carries on. What do you sell? PULSE offers what it read on your site (“From your website, we think you sell: …”). Choose Yes, that’s right or change it. Who usually buys from you? This is where your personas start. Where can people find you online? The pages found on your site are offered; tap the ones that are yours, or type an Instagram name or a LinkedIn page. Who else sells something similar? What do you want most right now? One of: Get more customers (the default), Get found on Google, Bring back past customers, Reach more people on social media, or Save time on posting. Want to show us your shop? Photos, a short video, a price list or a brochure, or a voice note. Each file says what PULSE could read from it. See what you can attach. Ready to check your business? Your answers as plain sentences; tap one to change it. More details (optional) holds the type of business, what you are best known for and anything else PULSE should know. Fine-tune the content ideas (optional) sets who you sell to, where you post and how deep the content research goes. Choose Start my check-up. It takes a few minutes. You can close the screen and carry on: the check-up keeps running, and the title line of every page shows how far it got. See what we found opens the result.
You can also start a check-up by typing one line to the assistant: Audit example.com. See Audit a domain.

data: There are two ways to run PULSE on your own machine. The Runink TIDE loop runs the whole stack: backend, inference, and the Flutter web app. The direct binary runs only the backend, which is enough to drive and test every non-AI RPC.
data.build#Build:
The generated Go protobuf code is not committed (grpc/api/v1/ is gitignored). Generate it from the repository root first, then build:
buf generate grpc/api/proto --template grpc/buf.gen.yaml -o grpc cd grpc && go build -o bin/pulse-server . && cd .. Run it from the repository root, with both the input path and --template, as written. Run from grpc/ it picks up a different configuration and the stubs land in the wrong place.
The Dart stubs under flutter/lib/core/grpc/ are committed, so you only need to regenerate them after changing a .proto. That is a second, separate run — see Developer guide.
data.option-1-the-tide-loop#Option 1: the TID:
From your TIDE checkout (the core directory):
cd ../core/grpc # TIDE's Go module; set PULSE_REPO to an absolute path for `dev up` PULSE_REPO=/abs/path/to/pulse go run ./cmd/tide dev up pulse This builds the backend and starts it on a free port. It starts the shared inference server when the model weights are present, then builds and serves the Flutter web app pointed at the backend’s real port. TIDE provisions the inference binaries and weights under ../core/artifacts/.
PULSE_REPO must be an absolute path. The built-in default is relative, and it resolves to nothing from TIDE’s Go module — the symptom is a build log with nothing in it.
data.prerequisites#Prerequisites: Go 1.26 (see grpc/go.mod). Flutter, with Dart 3.12 or newer (see flutter/pubspec.yaml), for the client. The sibling repositories checked out next to pulse/: core (Runink TIDE), inference, security, mesh, store, crawler, ui, and billing, plus ml, which ui needs. The backend does not build without them, because grpc/go.mod points at them with replace directives. buf and the local plugins protoc-gen-go and protoc-gen-go-grpc, to generate the Go protobuf code. The plugins must be on your PATH. grpcurl, to call the API by hand. SQLite is compiled in pure Go, so nothing here needs cgo.
data.run-the-flutter-client#Run the Flutter c:
cd flutter flutter run -d chrome # web flutter run -d linux # desktop flutter run # a connected Android device The client reads its backend address from PULSE_BACKEND_URL, a --dart-define. With no define, a native build talks to http://localhost:50051, and the web build resolves the address in order: the define, then a config.json served beside the app, then the origin the page came from. A define is baked in at compile time, which is why tide dev up rebuilds the web bundle when the backend port changes.
A deployment normally leaves the define empty: the backend serves the web bundle itself (PULSE_WEB_DIR), so the app and its gRPC-Web API are same-origin and no CORS entry is needed.
data.run-the-tests#Run the tests: cd grpc && TIDE_ENVELOPE_KEK="$(head -c32 /dev/urandom | base64 -w0)" go test ./... cd flutter && flutter analyze && flutter test
data.sign-in-and-call-an-rpc#Sign in and call: TOK=$(grpcurl -plaintext -d '{"username":"admin","password":""}' \ localhost:52000 pulse.v1.IdentityService/Login | jq -r '.accessToken') grpcurl -plaintext -H "authorization: Bearer $TOK" -d '{}' \ localhost:52000 pulse.v1.CampaignService/ListCampaigns The token is in the accessToken field, not token. A bearer token is how command-line and native clients authenticate; the web app never holds one and uses the session cookie instead. See Signing in.
data.start-the-server#Start the server:
cd grpc TIDE_ENVELOPE_KEK="$(openssl rand -base64 32)" \ PULSE_ADMIN_PASSWORD='' \ PULSE_JWT_SECRET="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" \ PULSE_GRPC_REFLECTION=true \ ./bin/pulse-server serve --port 52000 > /tmp/pulse.log 2>&1 & Four variables matter here:
PULSE_JWT_SECRET is required. Without it serve exits with refusing to start: no session signing key configured (PULSE_JWT_SECRET unset). There is no default and no generated key. Any value you generate works locally. It must never be a value that has been committed to a repository: PULSE refuses a key it recognises as published. TIDE_ENVELOPE_KEK is required too. It is the at-rest key that seals tokens in the database, and without it serve exits with Failed to initialize database: at-rest encryption key unavailable, refusing to start. A fresh random key works locally. PULSE_ADMIN_PASSWORD seeds a break-glass admin whose login username is admin unless PULSE_ADMIN_USERNAME says otherwise. Without it the log says skipping admin seed; break-glass login unavailable, no password is invented, and every password login fails. The seeded admin’s password is reset to the injected one on every restart. PULSE_GRPC_REFLECTION=true turns on gRPC server reflection so grpcurl can list services. It is off by default. Never set it on a deployed instance. With no --port (and no PORT variable), the server picks a free port.
Don’t stop the server with pkill -f 'pulse-server serve'. That pattern also matches the shell running the command, so it kills your own command and looks like a server crash. Kill the process by its PID instead.
data.wait-for-health#Wait for health: until curl -s localhost:52000/health | grep -q '"status":"ok"'; do sleep 2; done curl -s localhost:52000/health The response looks like {"status":"ok","model_ready":false,"port":52000}. model_ready stays false until an inference server has loaded its weights. The HTTP status is always 200. PULSE serves every non-AI feature without a model.
data.without-a-model#Without a model: A bare machine has no mistralrs-server and no model weights. The server still starts and serves login, every read, and every create or update. AI calls fail with inference server is not running. That is the expected result, not a bug.

data: PULSE has two ways in: Sign in with Google, and a username and password. Your PULSE shows the ones its administrator turned on.
data.how-long-you-stay-signed-in#How long you: In a browser, you stay signed in for up to 24 hours, then sign in again. The browser never holds your sign-in where a page script could read it. In the Android or Linux app, the app renews your sign-in by itself for up to 30 days. It keeps it in the device’s secure store, never in a plain file. Sign out is at the foot of the navigation rail. It ends that sign-in everywhere it is used at once.
data.sign-in-with-google#Sign in with Google: The button appears only when your PULSE has Google sign-in set up. Your Google address must be on your PULSE’s list of allowed addresses; if it is not, you see this account is not authorized for this instance. The first time you sign in with Google, PULSE makes you an account with the viewer role, unless an administrator gave your address a role in advance.
data.username-and-password#Username and passw: Sign in with your username, not your email address. A wrong username or password, or an account that has no password (accounts made through Google sign-in have none), answers invalid credentials.
data.what-your-role-lets-you-do#What your rol: Role What it can do Viewer Read everything in your account. Cannot start a check-up, send, call or publish. Editor Everything a viewer can, plus run check-ups, make and approve content, send email and place AI calls (where your administrator allows them). Admin Everything, plus Admin (members and roles) and the messaging settings, reached from Settings → Account. Ask an administrator to change your role. The server checks your role on every action, so a button you can see is not a promise that the action is allowed. Administrators: see Users and access.
data.where-the-session-lives#Where the sessio:
For administrators and developers.
Client What it holds Where Android, Linux An access token (24 hours) and a single-use refresh token (7 days), sent as authorization: Bearer … The platform keystore. There is no plaintext fallback: if the keystore refuses the write, the session lasts only until the app closes. Web Nothing The backend sets __Host-pulse_session, an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookie scoped to the exact host. The sign-in response carries no token, and no refresh token is issued. A cookie-authenticated call must also carry the header x-pulse-csrf: 1 and an Origin the server trusts: its own host, PULSE_PUBLIC_BASE_URL, or an exact entry of CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS (never a wildcard). The session behind the tokens lasts at most 30 days. See also Users and access and the HTTP endpoints.

data: Runink PULSE: Prescriptive Unified Lead & Social Engine does its AI work through a small set of agents. Each one has its own instructions, its own limits, and its own guardrails, but they all run on the same model server. A model card says, in plain language, what one agent does, what it reads, what it produces, who checks its work, and where it stops.
data.the-cards#The cards: Agent What you meet it as Diagnostic analyst The written diagnosis from a Site Audit, and the metrics read-out Market radar Radar research, competitor channels, and guest spots Strategy planner Recalculating the route of a 30-day follow-up cycle Channel content creator Posts, emails, outreach drafts, and the shorter Studio pieces Long-form studio Whitepapers, blog posts, and the weekly audiobook Partnership outreach First-contact messages to podcasts, channels, and brands Sales and voice agent Cold-call scripts, live replies on a phone call, and churn watch Content strategy and roadmaps Content pillars and phased roadmaps PULSE assistant The chat on every screen Self-healing operations agent Keeps PULSE’s own services running; the one agent that acts automatically, with an off switch
data.what-every-agent-has-in-common#What ever:
The model. Every request goes to the platform’s own model router, which sends it to a tier served by Distro-built mistral.rs on Runink’s inference servers: the general tier for writing, a judge tier for the plan gate, a vision tier for attached photos and video frames, and a reranker tier for ordering context. The models are open-weight (Qwen-family on the general tier). An agent’s own configuration sets its instructions and its sampling parameters, never its weights; content skills name their sampling in their SKILL.md. No plan routes to a different or “smarter” model. See Sovereign inference.
Where it runs. On the deployment’s own inference server: Runink’s shared machines on the Lite plan, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. PULSE calls no outside AI service on any plan. Some agents read the public web or your connected accounts while they work, and PULSE talks to the services you connect (HubSpot, LinkedIn, Google Analytics and others) as described in Connections.
Text in, text out. The agents read and write text. No agent generates images: there is no image-generation tier. Carousel slides and the frames of the Reels and Stories PULSE makes are drawn by PULSE itself in Go from the agent’s text, and videos are assembled with ffmpeg, with speech from TIDE’s ttsd. See Studio.
Grounded, or honest about not being. An agent that makes claims is given real material first: pages read live from the web, your connected accounts, and — for documents about Runink’s own products — the product corpus, searched by grep and read file by file, with no embeddings and no vector index. When nothing relevant is found, the agent is told so and writes without it, rather than filling the gap. See Sovereign inference.
Guardrails before the model. Before any agent is called, PULSE checks the request against a shared set of safety rules and refuses what they do not allow. Each agent’s card describes the commitments it keeps.
Outside text is data, not instructions. Web pages, search results, attached sources, lead and CRM records, inbound customer messages, and call transcripts reach an agent as material to read, never as instructions to follow.
Value first. Every agent that writes for an audience follows the same brand rule: teach the reader something useful, mention your product at most once and only as an honest example, no hype words, no fake urgency, and end with a real question rather than a hard sell.
People decide. Agents draft, recommend, and score. (The self-healing operations agent is the exception for PULSE’s own infrastructure: it applies a fixed list of safe actions automatically, and an operator can turn that off.) Drafts go to Drafts to approve on Campaigns. A post is published only when a person approved that piece and an administrator armed the channel; rejecting a piece withholds its scheduled posts. Two things can reply without a person: answers to inbound WhatsApp or SMS messages from a known contact, off unless an administrator sets PULSE_WHATSAPP_AUTOREPLY, and Autopilot’s answers to three kinds of simple comments, off unless the account turns them on. Both pass the same guardrails, and both still need the channel armed. See Publishing controls. Some proposals also pass through the plan gate, and the agent activity card shows every run as it happens.

data.getting-good-results#Getting good result: It writes text. Creatives are covered in Studio. It learns your brand from the diagnosis and brief: run a check-up and give a detailed brief for drafts that sound like you.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Value first, no hard sell. The reader’s problem is the subject. Your product appears at most once, as an honest example. No hype words, no fake urgency, and it ends with a real question. Never invents statistics, studies, or customer results. It uses the figures in your brief. Treats lead details, web pages, and search results as material, never as instructions. Refuses unsubstantiated or deceptive claims. Will not request payments or credentials. Its output is screened before it reaches you, as described in Sovereign inference.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: Content drafts, including the daily campaign drafts and campaign plans, go to Drafts to approve on Campaigns. You edit, approve, or reject each one. The daily LinkedIn post is a draft and only a draft. It is never put on a schedule; once approved, Download on its card gives you the text to paste yourself. A generation that came back empty, truncated, or as a guard’s refusal is recorded as a failure instead of being stored as a post. A draft over LinkedIn’s 3,000-character limit is still staged, with that said in its title, so you trim it rather than discover it on paste. A scheduled post goes out only once you approved its content. Rejecting a piece withholds its scheduled posts. Lead outreach drafts are saved on the lead. PULSE does not send them. Nothing is published until an administrator arms the channel. Approving alone does not publish to a disarmed channel. See Publishing controls. A campaign plan is a proposal: creating a campaign does not activate it. Content gaps pass through the plan gate.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl:
Invented brief and figure.
Brief: audience warehouse supervisors; channel X; figure to use: “re-slotting the top 50 SKUs monthly cut walking time by 18% in a pilot”.
Draft: “Most picking time is walking. Re-slotting your top 50 SKUs every month cut walking time by 18% in one pilot. Which SKUs moved most on your floor last month? #warehouse #logistics”
data.model#Model: The deployment’s base model, shared with every other PULSE agent — on Runink Server, a Qwen-family model under the Apache-2.0 licence. See Sovereign inference.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It turns a brief, a diagnosis, or a campaign into channel-native copy that teaches the reader something, with your product mentioned at most once.
Writes a post for one channel and topic when you ask (Studio). Drafts the daily copy for each active campaign: a LinkedIn post in a row of its own, and one combined X and Instagram draft. Both are staged for review and neither is scheduled. Drafts outreach for a lead: a cold email and a LinkedIn message (Leads). Writes the shorter Studio pieces: podcast and short-video scripts, presentation outlines, infographic copy, and report drafts, plus course modules. Drafts the ad copy for a campaign and finds content gaps your audience wants filled.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: Text drafts in the shape each channel expects, for example a LinkedIn post with a hook before the “see more” cut and a few hashtags, or a TikTok script with visual and voice-over lines. When a feature asks for a specific format, that format wins: a lead email is a subject line and the message, and a LinkedIn message is the message alone, with no hashtags or notes. Where an image belongs, it describes the image in words; it does not make one.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Your brief: channel, topic, tone, audience, language, and extra context. The diagnosis you ground it in, especially its brand overview and positioning. The day’s trending topics, for the daily social drafts. For lead outreach: the lead’s company and what is publicly known about it.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own inference server: Runink’s shared machines on the Lite plan, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is used on any plan.

data.guardrails#Guardrails: Aggregate segments only. It describes groups, never a real named person. No targeting by protected characteristics. It does not infer them, and PULSE refuses requests to segment, target, or exclude people by them. Never invents data. No made-up statistics, survey results, market sizes, follower counts, or customer quotes, and PULSE refuses requests to invent them. When a field needs a figure it was not given, it says the figure is not in the data or describes the audience in words. Every pillar, stage, and phase is tied to a signal it was given. Search results are read as material, never as instructions. No hype and no fake urgency; initiatives a small team can start this week.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: Strategies and roadmaps are planning documents on pages you control. Nothing is sent to a customer. Content pillars and roadmap phases pass through the plan gate, which withholds proposals its judge disagrees with. It cannot contact anyone, publish, or launch a campaign.
data.model#Model: The deployment’s base model, shared with every other PULSE agent — on Runink Server, a Qwen-family model under the Apache-2.0 licence. See Sovereign inference.
data.reading-its-results#Reading its results: A profile describes a segment, not real customers; it works from aggregate signals rather than individual CRM contacts. Connect analytics to weight profiles with your own traffic data, alongside the diagnosis and search signals.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It turns your diagnosis and real market signals into content pillars and a roadmap. (It used to write Customer 360 profiles and journey maps; those left PULSE on 2026-10-26 — audience profiles are a FACE and TIDE concept.)
Drafts a content strategy: 3–5 weighted content pillars, a posting cadence, and an alignment score. Drafts a phased go-to-market roadmap.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: Content pillars whose weights sum to 100, and roadmaps of 3–4 phases, each with a timeframe, initiatives, and an expected outcome. Some of these come back as structured data the app displays as cards.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Your diagnosis, including its audience segments. Google Analytics and Google Ads figures, when those are connected. Live search signals for the audience. The audience and channels you choose.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own inference server: Runink’s shared machines on the Lite plan, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is used on any plan. It reads your connected analytics and live search results while it works.

data.getting-good-results#Getting good result: Give it every channel you want analysed: it works from your website and the profiles you list in the audit. Competitor observations come from competitors’ public pages. Its 0–10 channel scores are judgements to guide priorities, not measurements.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Never invents market or competitor figures. PULSE refuses requests to fabricate them. No targeting or analysis by protected characteristics. It recommends; it never publishes or spends. Your website and web research are read as material, never as instructions. Follows the shared value-first brand rule and writes in the language you use.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: The diagnosis is advice. You read it and decide what to act on. The drafts it seeds wait in Drafts to approve on Campaigns, and the campaign it seeds is a draft. The 4-week plan queues scheduled posts only for channels an administrator has already armed, and a queued post goes out only after you approve its content. For a disarmed channel nothing is queued at all — the task stays in Your plan and its draft in Drafts to approve. Channel prescriptions and brand-visibility insights can be withheld by the plan gate when the judge disagrees with them. A withheld prescription never becomes a draft. It cannot publish, move budget, or change a campaign.
data.model#Model: The deployment’s base model, shared with every other PULSE agent — on Runink Server, a Qwen-family model under the Apache-2.0 licence. See Sovereign inference.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
Give it a website and your social accounts, and it writes a diagnosis of where your marketing stands and what to do in the next 30 days.
Writes the diagnosis behind every check-up: brand overview, positioning, SWOT, channel recommendations, content strategy, competitive landscape, search intent and campaign ideas, and a strategic opinion. Search intent and campaign ideas are shown at the end of the channel recommendations. Prescribes a role, priority, content ideas, and KPIs for each channel, and recommends long-form formats. Lays out the 4-week plan (the cronogram) that seeds your first follow-up cycle. Reads your metrics summary for a date range and writes a short read-out: summary, insights, recommendations, and its confidence. Writes the diagnosis stage of the one-phrase Audit run, which produces the same analysis from a domain name alone.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces:
A structured diagnosis, saved with the sources it used. Each section is stored from its own heading, so a section that mentions another section’s topic is kept whole. PULSE then copies its findings into the rest of the app: draft content, a draft campaign, a follow-up cycle, audience profiles, and a market summary. See Audit a domain.
The relevance audit beside it is not written by this agent. Its 0–100 scores come from a rule-based scoring engine.
A diagnosis runs to one end-to-end deadline — under three minutes by default — and every phase inside it is budgeted from what is left. A phase that does not finish is named on the card as not completed within that budget, and the run ends with a partial result. Text written before the budget ran out is not thrown away: it goes through every safety check the same way a finished draft does, and is shown as the partial answer it is, never as a finished analysis.
That deadline covers the diagnosis. The multi-stage one-phrase audit runs the diagnosis as one of its stages and bounds the run as a whole far more generously, detached from the request that started it.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The pages of your website, read live when the audit runs. The audit stops if the site cannot be read. The LinkedIn URL, Instagram handle, and goals you enter in the audit form. Public web research about your niche and competitors. Your business profile, and Google Analytics or Google Ads signals when those are connected. For the metrics read-out: the follower, impression, engagement, click, lead, and conversion figures PULSE has synced.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own inference server: Runink’s shared machines on the Lite plan, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is used on any plan. Reading your website and researching your niche means PULSE fetches public web pages while the audit runs.

data.getting-good-results#Getting good result: It writes from the brief and the product corpus, so a detailed brief gives a richer piece. Very long documents follow the deployment’s time budget; see Sovereign inference. It writes text; audio comes from the platform’s text-to-speech.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Value first, no hard sell. It teaches the topic; your product appears at most once, as an honest example, never as the headline. Facts only from the brief and the corpus. Every capability claim has to trace to a passage it was given. It never invents statistics, studies, quotes, customer names, or case results. If a point needs a number it was not given, it makes the point without one. No verified source, said out loud. When the corpus has nothing on the topic, the agent is told so explicitly and writes from the topic and industry alone, rather than inventing capabilities, integrations, certifications, customers, or partnerships. No hype words, no clichés, no fake urgency. Will not handle payments or credentials. Its output is screened before it reaches you.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: You edit and approve every piece. Saved pieces wait in Drafts to approve on Campaigns like any other content. Blog posts, podcast episodes, and the audiobook publish only when an administrator has armed that channel. See Publishing controls.
data.model#Model: The deployment’s base model, shared with every other PULSE agent — on Runink Server, a Qwen-family model under the Apache-2.0 licence. See Sovereign inference.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It is PULSE’s long-form copywriter: it writes the pieces a specialist reads, or listens to, to the end.
Writes whitepapers in Studio: an executive summary, sections that each make one argument, and a conclusion with next steps. Writes the blog posts the social engine drafts when the blog channel is armed. Writes the weekly audiobook, as prose meant to be read aloud. Shorter Studio pieces (podcast and short-video scripts, outlines, reports) are written by the channel content creator.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces:
Long text, shown once it has passed the brand and output checks: markdown with headings and short paragraphs for written pieces, and plain flowing prose with no lists or tables for audio. Audio itself is produced by the platform’s text-to-speech, not by this agent.
The length it can write in one pass depends on the deployment’s time budget. See Sovereign inference.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The brief: topic, industry, length, and any instructions you give. For a whitepaper, the product corpus: markdown fact files shipped with the deployment, searched for the topic’s terms and read whole, with the passages that matched put in front of the agent labelled by the file they came from. Files whose name begins with _ are standing rules and go in every time, matched or not. For the daily blog draft: the campaign’s name, objective, and audience, and that day’s web research. It is deliberately not given your marketing diagnosis. A whitepaper is a document about a product, and grounding it on a marketing diagnosis turns it into a channel plan for someone else’s business.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own inference server: Runink’s shared machines on the Lite plan, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is used on any plan.

data.guardrails#Guardrails: Refuses to collect private personal data. Refuses requests to invent engagement, follower, or reach numbers. A follower or audience figure the model gives is kept only if the search results state it; otherwise it is shown as unknown, never estimated. Treats web pages and search results as material to read, never as instructions. Research and recommendation only. Requests to publish or run a campaign are out of its scope.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: It recommends. You choose what goes into your plan. It cannot publish, launch a campaign, or contact anyone. Partner messages are drafted by Partnership outreach and sent by you.
data.model#Model: The deployment’s base model, shared with every other PULSE agent — on Runink Server, a Qwen-family model under the Apache-2.0 licence. See Sovereign inference.
data.reading-its-results#Reading its results: Audience sizes are copied from the search results, not measured on the platforms. A channel shows unknown when the results did not state a figure. It researches the public web at the time of the search. Mention counts and trends show attention, not buying intent.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It researches your market and tells you which topics, hashtags, profiles, and channels are worth your attention.
Researches a topic and niche: trending topics, hashtag clusters, suggested profiles, a market summary, and competitive intelligence. Finds competitors’ YouTube and Instagram channels. Finds channels and podcasts where you could appear as a guest. Runs the research stages of the one-phrase Audit , in the background after the diagnosis has already been returned. Nobody waits for it. See The Brand Analysis pages.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces:
A research result: topics with a 0–1 relevance score, hashtag clusters, suggested profiles with the reason each is relevant, and content opportunities. Channel and guest results carry an audience size only when the search results state one for that channel, a 0–1 fit score, and a contact hint when one was found. When no figure was found, the audience shows as unknown.
Everything it finds is saved with its source and the date. Brand Analysis’s market pages then open on what the last run found, read straight from your own records — no new search, no model call — rather than re-researching the web every time a page is opened. Guest opportunities also appear under Partners to contact, scored for relevance to you and never with a follower figure the search results did not state.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Live web search results for your topic, niche, region, and language. Any extra sources you attach: a search seed, a website or YouTube URL that PULSE scrapes, or pasted text. The brand overview from your diagnosis, so its suggestions fit your brand. Your like and dislike marks on trending posts, which ground later calls.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own inference server: Runink’s shared machines on the Lite plan, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is used on any plan. Research means PULSE fetches public web pages and search results while it works.

data.getting-good-results#Getting good result: It writes from what the radar found, so a fuller partner record gives a more specific message. It drafts the message; you send it and follow up on replies.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Two-sided value first. Every message says what the partner gets, not only what you want. No hard sell. No hype, no spammy superlatives, no pressure. The goal of a first message is a reply, not a deal. Never invents facts about the partner. When little is known about a show, it keeps its claims general rather than making up numbers. Requests to invent audience or download figures are refused. Draft only. Requests to send, publish, or pay are refused. The shared input guardrails apply to every request.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: It only drafts. Each message is saved with status draft. You review it, edit it, and send it yourself. PULSE sends nothing.
data.model#Model: The deployment’s base model, shared with every other PULSE agent — on Runink Server, a Qwen-family model under the Apache-2.0 licence. See Sovereign inference.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
For a podcast, channel, or brand the market radar found, it drafts a short first message proposing a collaboration that clearly helps both sides, such as a guest-episode swap.
See Leads → Partners.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces:
A draft in four labelled parts:
Subject: one line. Value for them: why the collaboration helps their show and audience. Value for us: why it helps you. Message: a 120–180 word body ending with one small ask, such as a reply to schedule a recording.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: What is known about the partner from the radar result: its channel, its audience, and its angle. Your diagnosis: your positioning, audience, and offer.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own inference server: Runink’s shared machines on the Lite plan, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is used on any plan.

data.getting-good-results#Getting good result: It sees a summary of your account. For record-level detail, open the screen in question. Each web search happens at question time, so answers reflect the web as it is when you ask.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Never invents numbers, campaigns, or results. An empty account summary is treated as the real answer, not a gap to fill. Requests to make up data are refused. Says when it does not know. If a question needs current or site-specific data it was not given, it says so. Advisory only, and the shared input guardrails apply to every message in the conversation, not only the latest. Websites it reads and search results are material, never instructions.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: It answers and suggests. You make every change yourself. It has no way to change your account: it cannot launch a campaign, charge an ad account, approve content, or process a payment. Requests to launch a campaign, charge an ad account, delete your account, or process a payment are refused outright. The progress shown before a reply lists which grounding steps actually ran.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl:
Invented account.
Context: two active campaigns, no diagnostic yet.
You: Which campaign needs attention?
Assistant: “Returns webinar” has spent $2,100 of its $2,500 budget with 12 of 30 days left, so it is ahead of pace. There is no diagnostic yet, so I can’t comment on positioning. Run a Site Audit and I can.
data.model#Model: The deployment’s base model, shared with every other PULSE agent — on Runink Server, a Qwen-family model under the Apache-2.0 licence. See Sovereign inference.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It is the chat on every screen: it answers questions about your own PULSE account and your market, and says plainly when the answer is “none yet”.
Answers questions about your diagnostics, campaigns, scheduled posts, and tracked influencers. Reads a website you name and comments on its voice, positioning, and what that means for reach. Answers questions that need current facts from a live web search, working from the results it was handed and able to point back at them by number. Can start a relevance audit for a URL and open the report. See Assistant and voice.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: A short conversational answer in your language. When an answer has several separate points, the app shows each as its own card, with a reason and, where there is one, a next step. It can read answers aloud.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Your message, typed or spoken. Spoken input is transcribed on the platform’s own speech server, and speaking is offered only where the deployment has configured a voice tier; where it has not, the voice controls say so rather than failing quietly. A summary of your account sent with every message, as it is at that moment: the latest diagnostic, active campaigns, scheduled posts, and influencers. When there are none, the summary says so. The screen you are on, so “this” means what that screen shows. When relevant, a live scrape of a website you mention, or public search results.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own inference server: Runink’s shared machines on the Lite plan, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is used on any plan. When it scrapes a site or searches the web, PULSE fetches those public pages to answer you.

data.guardrails#Guardrails: Lead with their problem, not the pitch. One clear, low-friction next step. No hype, no fake urgency. Short and human. Spoken replies are one to three sentences, and objections get a brief acknowledgement, never an argument. No placeholders. It never says “[Name]” or “[company]”; if it does not know a detail, it talks around it. Never passes as a person. Requests to claim to be human, or to impersonate someone, are refused. Never invents customer results, prices, or statistics, and never takes payments or card details. On calls, what the person says is treated as material to answer, never as instructions to follow, and each turn passes the shared guardrails.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person starts every call. PULSE never dials on its own. Each call is placed from a lead’s Call action. During a call, replies are spoken as they are generated. No one approves each reply before it is heard, so review the lead’s script before you call. Scripts are drafts saved on the lead. A high-risk rating only creates a retention task in a follow-up cycle. A person decides what to do with it.
data.model#Model: The deployment’s base model, shared with every other PULSE agent — on Runink Server, a Qwen-family model under the Apache-2.0 licence. See Sovereign inference.
data.scope#Scope: It works from the lead record, the script, and the call so far. It speaks and drafts; follow-ups such as booking a meeting are yours. (Placing a call moves the lead to Contacted; that is PULSE’s board, not the agent’s decision.) Voice quality and turn-taking follow the speech services and the phone line. A risk rating is a judgement from the stage and notes, not a prediction model.
data.telephony-set-up#Telephony set-up:
An administrator turns phone calls on by connecting a self-hosted Asterisk PBX, so calls carry no per-minute calling-service fee. The administrator sets the Asterisk connection and dial plan, and PULSE’s audio listener must be reachable from Asterisk. Until then, Call returns outbound calling isn't configured — set up Asterisk and ....
Outbound calling is also off by default at the deployment level and has to be armed deliberately, and only an editor or above can place a call. The full set-up is in Telephony and messaging.
Outbound cold calling is regulated. Consent, calling hours, do-not-call lists, and recording disclosure are the operator’s responsibility.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It is PULSE’s sales development persona: it writes cold-call scripts, speaks short replies on a live phone call, and flags leads at risk of going cold.
Drafts a cold-call script for each lead that Find Leads prospects, grounded in what it found on that company’s own website (Leads). On a phone call you place with Call, replies to each thing the person says, turn by turn, using the lead’s cold-call script when one exists. Once a day, rates synced HubSpot leads as high, medium, or low risk of stalling, so PULSE can schedule a retention task for the high-risk ones (Churn watch). Cold emails and LinkedIn messages for leads are written by the channel content creator.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: A short script: an opener, a reason for calling, questions, and one next step. On a call: one to three natural spoken sentences per turn, with no lists or formatting, read out by the platform’s text-to-speech. For churn watch: a single risk rating per lead.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: For a script: the lead’s name, title, and company, and, for prospected leads, gaps found on the lead’s website. For churn watch: the lead’s name, company, stage, and notes. Your diagnosis, to ground the pitch in your positioning. On a call: the transcript of what the person just said. Speech-to-text runs on the platform’s own speech server.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own inference server, with speech-to-text and text-to-speech on the platform’s own speech services: Runink’s shared machines on the Lite plan, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is used on any plan. The phone call itself travels through your Asterisk PBX and whatever phone carrier it connects to.

data.guardrails#Guardrails: Never destructive. No deleting data, dropping tables, shutting down hosts, or rolling back releases; its rollback only undoes its own recent change. Requests that point it that way are refused, and nothing is applied. Never touches security controls: authentication, encryption, certificates, secrets, firewalls, network policies, guardrails, or audit logs. What it reads about a failing component is treated as data, never as instructions.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: Automatic by default, with an off switch. An operator can turn automatic remediation off with one setting. Plans are then still recorded, but nothing is applied. Unsure means notify. A plan below a confidence floor, or anything outside the fixed list, becomes a notification and changes nothing. Every event and its outcome are shown in the system health view and the logs.
data.model#Model: The deployment’s base model, on the same inference server as every other PULSE agent. It runs under its own operations instructions, separate from the marketing agents, and at a near-deterministic sampling setting, so two identical events do not get two different decisions.
data.scope#Scope: It acts on PULSE’s own components. The shared inference server and other applications are run by their own operators. Adding capacity stops at a set ceiling; past it, the problem goes to an operator.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It keeps PULSE’s own services running. When PULSE detects that one of its components is under pressure or unreachable, this agent picks one remediation from a short, fixed list, and PULSE applies it.
This is the one agent that acts without a person approving each step. It never writes for customers and never touches your marketing data.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces:
One plan: an action from the fixed list, the component it applies to, a one-sentence reason, and a confidence.
The fixed list:
Restart one of PULSE’s model services. Add capacity to one of PULSE’s model services, within a set ceiling. Pause failing calls for a short time, so they stop piling up. This resumes by itself. Roll back its own most recent change to a component, and only when that change happened shortly before the fault. It never rolls back a release, a deployment, or data, and never undoes a change someone else made. Notify: change nothing, and record the event for an operator.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: A health event raised by PULSE’s own monitoring: what is affected, how severe it is, and what was observed.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: Inside the deployment. It reads PULSE’s own health signals only. No third-party AI service is used.

data.getting-good-results#Getting good result: Log your check-ins: each recalculation works from them, so regular check-ins give a sharper route. Targets are planning aids, not forecasts.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Refuses requests to invent KPI results or check-in data. It works from the numbers you entered. Will not endorse unsustainable work patterns. Plans include rest days. It does not know your calendar, so tell it in a check-in note if your time is limited. Planning only. Requests to publish or run a diagnosis are out of its scope. Follows the shared value-first brand rule.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: The revised plan is a recommendation. You decide what to change. It cannot write or publish posts, run a diagnosis, or move budget.
data.model#Model: The deployment’s base model, shared with every other PULSE agent — on Runink Server, a Qwen-family model under the Apache-2.0 licence. See Sovereign inference.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It keeps your 30-day plan realistic: when you ask, it recalculates the route from how your weekly check-ins have moved.
Reviews the check-in history of a follow-up cycle week over week. Says what is working, what to change, and what to drop, and why. Adjusts the content mix, the effort per channel, and the KPI targets to your actual trajectory. The first plan of a cycle comes from the diagnostic analyst. This agent revises it. See Your plan.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: A revised plan, shown once it has passed the brand and output checks: weekly themes and goals, daily tasks with a channel, type, time estimate, and priority, KPI targets with an optimistic and a conservative figure, and the adjustments it made, each tied to the check-in numbers that triggered it.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The follow-up cycle and its planner tasks, with their status. Your weekly check-ins: new followers, posts, engagements, leads, satisfaction, and your notes on what worked and what did not. Your latest diagnosis, including its brand overview.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own inference server: Runink’s shared machines on the Lite plan, your own cloud or servers on Dedicated and Enterprise. No outside AI service is used on any plan.

data:
Runink PULSE: Prescriptive Unified Lead & Social Engine writes and publishes in your brand’s name, so it starts by learning who you are and which accounts it may read from or publish to. Each person does that under Settings. Some connections also need one-time work by the administrator of the PULSE instance in a platform’s developer console: those pages say exactly what to set.
Business profileName, industry, timezone, language, tone, active channels. ConnectionsEvery card under Settings › Integrations, and what each one unlocks. Public address and redirectsPULSE_PUBLIC_BASE_URL, the three sign-in callbacks, the TIDE edge. Meta (Instagram)META_APP_ID / META_APP_SECRET, permissions and app review. GoogleOne OAuth client: YouTube, Search Console, Gmail, Google sign-in. LinkedInLINKEDIN_CLIENT_ID / SECRET, products, company pages. Website repositoryA fine-grained GitHub token for one repository; fixes as pull requests. EmailEach person’s own mailbox: Gmail, Microsoft 365 or SMTP. VoiceTTSD_URL: TIDE’s shared speech service.
data.what-needs-which-connection#What needs w: Feature Needs Brand Analysis (the audit, the diagnosis, content ideas), Campaigns, Studio drafts Nothing: PULSE reads your public site and writes with its own model Search demand in Brand Analysis and plans Google Search Console Publishing to Instagram, and reading its results, comments, mentions and messages Meta Publishing to YouTube, and reading its results and comments Google Publishing to LinkedIn, as yourself or a company page LinkedIn Fixes to your own website as pull requests Website repository Sending outreach email from your own address Email Voiceover on the Reels and Stories PULSE makes, read-back, podcasts Voice Lead sync and the WhatsApp sender allowlist HubSpot, see Connections Website traffic and forecasts Google Analytics, see Connections Ads performance Google Ads, see Connections A connection never publishes by itself. Whether anything may leave PULSE is decided by the administrator’s switches; see Switches and arming order.

data:
Settings › Account (/settings?tab=account) holds your profile, the appearance, and your business profile and content defaults. The page reads them with ConfigService.GetConfig and saves them with UpdateConfig. Nothing is saved until you choose Save changes.
Settings has four tabs: Account, Integrations (see Connections), Clients (for agencies) and Subscription (your plan and seats).
data.active-channels#Active channels:
Settings › Integrations is one grid of cards. Under Publish to, each channel PULSE can publish to (LinkedIn, Instagram, YouTube, Website, Podcast, Audiobook) has its account, an Active switch (saved with Save changes), and one status line: “Ready to publish”, or “Can’t publish” with the first reason. Tap the line for every reason and the channel’s recent dispatches. Switch names and user ids in those reasons are shown to admins only. Measure & CRM holds the read-only accounts (Google Analytics, Google Ads, HubSpot) in the same cards, without the switch.
Active is a real gate. An active channel is planned in the campaign roadmap and starts the content strategy’s channel picks. It gets PULSE’s daily drafts (the LinkedIn draft, the Instagram caption, the blog article, the podcast episode, the audiobook chapter, the YouTube Short) and may publish. A channel you turn off gets no drafts, and anything already queued for it is recorded withheld: channel not active instead of being sent. A new account starts with every channel PULSE can publish to active. Channels saved before Active became a gate (when the chips only meant focus) gained, once, every channel that could publish then (LinkedIn, YouTube, website, podcast, audiobook), so nothing that was publishing stopped. What may publish is also an administrator setting, armed channel by channel. See Publishing controls and which channels can publish.
data.business-profile#Business profile: Field Used for Business name How PULSE names your business Industry Context for analysis and generation Timezone Scheduling and dates
data.content-defaults#Content defaults: Field Choices Interface language System default, English, Spanish, French, Portuguese. This changes the app’s own labels. Default content language English, Spanish, French, Portuguese (Brazil) Default tone Professional, Casual, Friendly, Authoritative Each generation request sets its own language and tone. When a request leaves the tone empty, content generation uses professional.
data.stored-preferences#Stored preferences: AppConfig also has a free-form preferences map of string keys and values. The Settings page keeps whatever is stored there when it saves, but has no fields for it. API clients can set it.

data:
Settings › Integrations (/settings?tab=integrations) is one grid of cards, one per account or channel. Publish to holds the places PULSE can publish to; Measure & CRM holds the accounts it only reads. Every credential is your own, stored per user and sealed (encrypted) before it is written to the database. A card that needs the administrator to set something first says which setting is missing.
How each one connects:
Card How you connect Instagram, YouTube, LinkedIn Sign in at the platform (OAuth): Connect with Instagram, Connect with YouTube, Connect with LinkedIn Google Search Console Sign in with Google (OAuth, read-only): Connect Search Console Email Sign in with Google or Microsoft (OAuth), or your own SMTP server Website repository A fine-grained GitHub token limited to that one repository, entered by an administrator Website (blog publishing) A GitHub token Google Analytics, Google Ads A Google Cloud service-account key you create HubSpot A HubSpot Private App token
data.email#Email: Connect Gmail, Connect Microsoft 365 or an SMTP server: your own mailbox, so that Send on a lead’s email draft sends from your address. See Email.
data.google-ads#Google Ads:
Paste the JSON key of a service account with domain-wide delegation (scope adwords), the Ads Customer ID, a Developer Token, an optional Login Customer ID (manager account), and the Subject email the service account impersonates. All but the login customer ID are required.
Test on Google Analytics and Google Ads runs a real API call with PULSE’s own client.
data.google-analytics#Google Analytics: Paste the full JSON key of a Google Cloud service account that has access to the GA4 property, and the numeric Property ID (GA4 Admin › Property Settings). Both are required. It feeds website traffic and the forecasts. Without it, those places say Google Analytics isn't connected yet.
data.google-search-console#Google Search Cons: What people type into Google before they find your site. Connect Search Console signs in with Google, read-only, and PULSE reads clicks, impressions, click rate and position once a day. See Google.
data.hubspot#HubSpot: A HubSpot Private App token. It enables Sync Now on Leads, pushes new prospects to HubSpot, and backs the WhatsApp sender allowlist (see Telephony and messaging).
data.linkedin-instagram-and-youtube#LinkedIn,:
Each card offers Connect with LinkedIn, Connect with Instagram or Connect with YouTube when the administrator has set up the platform’s app (see LinkedIn, Meta, Google). You sign in at the platform and approve what PULSE asks for; PULSE stores the token, sealed, and renews it before it runs out where the platform allows. The card shows connected, expiring, expired, missing permission or not set up, the end date, and for each feature (publishing, results, comments, direct messages) whether the permission it needs was granted. Disconnect withdraws PULSE’s access at the platform where its API allows it, then deletes the stored tokens.
Fallback while sign-in is not set up. Until the administrator configures the platform’s app, the card says sign-in is not set up and accepts a token you created on the platform yourself. Test then asks the platform whose token it is: LinkedIn GET /v2/userinfo (it needs the openid and profile scopes, or the test fails with a 403) and Meta Graph GET /me.
On LinkedIn you can post as yourself or, when the administrator turned on company pages, as a page you administer.
data.podcast-and-audiobook#Podcast and Audiob: Episodes and chapters are published through PULSE’s own podcast feed, which podcast platforms poll. There is nothing to connect; the administrator sets the public address the feed needs.
data.website#Website: Blog posts reach your website as a pull request, or a commit, made with a GitHub personal access token stored on this card. The repository, branch and folder are set by the administrator (PULSE_SITE_REPO and friends); see Site pipeline.
data.website-form-and-samgov#Website form and:
The website form gives you a link your site’s contact form can post to, so enquiries become leads. See Website form. SAM.gov takes your own API key so Opportunities can read US federal tenders.
PULSE has no connector for X (Twitter), Mailchimp or TikTok. Connections to them saved by older versions are hidden and never tested.
data.website-repository#Website repository: Your site’s own GitHub repository, where PULSE proposes fixes from the site audit as pull requests for you to review and merge. An administrator connects it with a token limited to that one repository. See Website repository.
data.what-autopilot-reads-on-instagram-and-yo:
Autopilot reads results, comments, mentions and direct messages back with the same token publishing uses. Each needs a permission on that token; PULSE never assumes one is granted. When a platform refuses a read for a missing permission, the account shows Reconnect to allow … for that kind only (the rest keeps working), and the reply queue says the same. To re-consent, connect again with the platform’s sign-in, which asks for every permission below, or paste a new token that has them (it replaces the old one).
Platform Kind Permission / scope Instagram (Graph API with Facebook Login: a Meta token and the Instagram professional account ID) Results (reach, views, likes, comments, saves, shares where the post type reports them) instagram_basic, instagram_manage_insights, pages_read_engagement, pages_show_list Comments and replies; mentions (posts that tag the account) instagram_basic, instagram_manage_comments, pages_read_engagement, pages_show_list Direct messages and replies instagram_basic, instagram_manage_messages, pages_manage_metadata, pages_read_engagement, pages_show_list; the Instagram app setting Allow access to messages must be on YouTube (a Google access token and its refresh token) Publishing https://www.googleapis.com/auth/youtube.upload Views, likes, comment counts; comments and replies https://www.googleapis.com/auth/youtube.force-ssl Average view duration and percentage https://www.googleapis.com/auth/yt-analytics.readonly Every Meta permission above needs Advanced Access through Meta App Review (and business verification) before it works for accounts that have no role on the Meta app. The three Google scopes are sensitive scopes: the instance’s OAuth client needs Google’s verification before people outside the project can grant them. A reply to a direct message is sent only within 24 hours of the person’s last message (Meta’s messaging window); after that PULSE says so and sends nothing. YouTube has no mentions and no direct messages: the app says “not available on YouTube”. A figure a platform did not report for that kind of post is shown as not measured, never as 0.

data:
The Email card connects your own mailbox, so that Send on a lead’s email draft sends from your address. PULSE has no shared sender and uses no email service provider. Connect one of:
Option How it connects What PULSE may do Gmail Connect Gmail opens Google’s consent page (OAuth with PKCE). Send mail (gmail.send), your address (openid email), and read your mail (gmail.readonly) so PULSE can see who answered. PULSE keeps only a short snippet of each reply to an email it sent, never the message. Microsoft 365 Connect Microsoft 365 opens Microsoft’s consent page. Send mail as you (delegated Mail.Send), read your mail (Mail.Read) to see who answered, read your profile (User.Read), and stay connected (offline_access). SMTP Host, port (587 for STARTTLS, 465 for TLS), username, password and from address. PULSE logs in before saving. A server that does not offer STARTTLS is refused: no password or message is sent unencrypted. Tokens and the SMTP password are sealed in the integrations table like every other credential. Test asks the provider who the mailbox is and sends nothing: Google’s token check (which must show gmail.send), Graph GET /me, or an SMTP login. An expired Google or Microsoft token is refreshed once.
If several mailboxes are connected, PULSE sends from the most recently connected one that passed its check; the sheet names the address before you send.
data.for-the-administrator#For the administra:
Gmail and Microsoft 365 use the instance’s own OAuth clients, read from the instance configuration, never from a repository secret:
Set PULSE_PUBLIC_BASE_URL. The redirect URI is /oauth/mail/callback. Gmail: in the Google Cloud project behind GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID and GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET, enable the Gmail API, add the redirect URI to the web client, and add the gmail.send and gmail.readonly scopes to the consent screen (gmail.readonly is a restricted scope: Google requires app verification beyond 100 users). Microsoft 365: register an app in Microsoft Entra, add the redirect URI as a Web platform, grant the delegated Graph permissions Mail.Send, Mail.Read, User.Read and offline_access, create a client secret, and set MICROSOFT_CLIENT_ID, MICROSOFT_CLIENT_SECRET and, for a single-tenant app, MICROSOFT_TENANT_ID (default common). A connect link works once and for ten minutes.
SMTP needs nothing from the administrator: each person enters their own server. Sending by any route still needs PULSE_APPLY_ENABLED=true and PULSE_PUBLISH_EMAIL not set to false; PULSE_EMAIL_DAILY_LIMIT (50) caps each person’s sends per 24 hours. See Switches and arming order.
data.replies#Replies:
PULSE looks for answers to the emails it sent, every 15 minutes and each time you open Leads, for sends from the last 30 days. A reply is matched on the sent email’s own thread (Gmail) or conversation (Microsoft 365), so other mail is never matched. A lead who answered is marked replied and shows under To do today on Leads, with the first words of the answer and Answer, until you move it past Contacted. Only a short snippet (200 characters) is kept, sealed like every credential.
A Gmail or Microsoft 365 mailbox connected before reply tracking, or without the reading permission, is never read. The Email card and To do today say to Reconnect, which asks for the permission again. An SMTP mailbox has no inbox PULSE can read: replies are not tracked, and the page says so. (IMAP is not supported.)
data.what-send-does#What Send does:
Leads → Email → Send sends the newest saved draft to the lead, records the attempt (outreach_sends: lead, provider, provider message id, time, status) and moves a new lead to contacted. Nothing is sent automatically. Send is shown only when all of these hold; otherwise the sheet says which one is missing and keeps Copy and Open in email:
your account is an editor or admin; the administrator armed PULSE_APPLY_ENABLED and did not set PULSE_PUBLISH_EMAIL=false (see Switches); a mailbox is connected and its last check passed; you are under the daily limit (PULSE_EMAIL_DAILY_LIMIT, 50 by default). Outreach from the sheet is one-to-one, so it carries no List-Unsubscribe header. A marketing send through the API (marketing=true) adds one.

data: For the administrator. One Google OAuth web client serves Google sign-in, Connect with YouTube, Connect Search Console and Connect Gmail. Its id and secret are GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID and GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET, set on the PulseControlPlane from the instance’s secret store, never from a repository secret. Google Analytics and Google Ads do not use this client: each person pastes a service-account key (see Connections).
data.gmail#Gmail: Connect Gmail asks for gmail.send, openid email, and gmail.readonly so PULSE can see who answered. See Email.
data.google-sign-in#Google sign-in: With GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID set, the login screen offers Google sign-in. Who may sign in is AUTH_ALLOWED_EMAILS (empty means nobody); AUTH_GOOGLE_ONLY=true hides the password form. See Users and access.
data.in-the-google-cloud-console#In the Googl:
In the project that owns the OAuth client, enable the APIs for what you want people to connect:
API For YouTube Data API v3 Publishing, statistics, comments and replies YouTube Analytics API Average view duration and percentage Google Search Console API Search Console Gmail API Sending from Gmail and seeing replies Create (or open) the OAuth client of type Web application and add the redirect URIs, each under your https PULSE_PUBLIC_BASE_URL: /oauth/social/callback (YouTube), /oauth/search-console/callback (Search Console) and /oauth/mail/callback (Gmail). See Public address and redirects. For Google sign-in in the browser, Google also requires the app’s origin under Authorized JavaScript origins.
On the OAuth consent screen, add the scopes below.
Submit the app for verification. The YouTube scopes and webmasters.readonly are sensitive scopes and gmail.readonly is a restricted one: until Google verifies the app, only test users of the project can grant them (and restricted scopes are capped at 100 users).
data.search-console#Search Console: Connect Search Console asks only for https://www.googleapis.com/auth/webmasters.readonly (with PKCE and offline access), then lists the properties the Google account can read. PULSE picks the one that matches the audited site, otherwise the person chooses. Once a day it reads clicks, impressions, click rate and average position per search and per page for the last 28 days and the 28 before (Google’s figures lag about two days). It spends at most 25 Search Console calls per account a day, manual reads included; a quota answer from Google is recorded and the read is retried the next day. Not connected, every place that would show these figures says “not measured”.
data.youtube#YouTube:
Connect with YouTube asks for:
https://www.googleapis.com/auth/youtube.upload (publishing); https://www.googleapis.com/auth/youtube.force-ssl (views, likes, comment counts, comments and replies); https://www.googleapis.com/auth/yt-analytics.readonly (average view duration and percentage). PULSE stores the access and refresh tokens sealed and renews the access token shortly before it expires. A scope the person did not grant is listed on the card. YouTube has no mentions and no direct messages through its API; the app says “not available on YouTube”. Uploads are private unless YOUTUBE_PRIVACY_STATUS says unlisted or public. Publishing also needs PULSE_APPLY_ENABLED and PULSE_PUBLISH_YOUTUBE.
Without the client, the YouTube card accepts a pasted Google access token and its refresh token instead.

data: For the administrator: what to set up so people can press Connect with LinkedIn, and optionally post as a company page. Without it, the LinkedIn card accepts a pasted token instead.
data.in-pulse#In PULSE:
Setting What to set LINKEDIN_CLIENT_ID, LINKEDIN_CLIENT_SECRET The app’s client id and secret (the secret from the instance’s secret store). With both and an https PULSE_PUBLIC_BASE_URL, the card shows Connect with LinkedIn. LINKEDIN_COMPANY_PAGES true only after LinkedIn approved the Community Management API. The card then also offers Connect company pages, which asks for the three page scopes and lists the pages the member administers to post as. LinkedIn access tokens last 60 days. PULSE renews one in its last ten days only when LinkedIn issued a refresh token (LinkedIn does that only for apps it enabled for programmatic refresh); otherwise the card shows “reconnect before” the date. Disconnect revokes the token at LinkedIn, then deletes it.
Connecting publishes nothing. LinkedIn posts also need PULSE_APPLY_ENABLED, PULSE_PUBLISH_LINKEDIN and the content owner in PULSE_PUBLISHER_USER_IDS; the daily LinkedIn draft is never scheduled by itself. See Switches and arming order.
data.in-the-linkedin-developer-portal#In the: Create an app, associated with the company’s LinkedIn page. Under Auth, add /oauth/social/callback to the authorized redirect URLs (see Public address and redirects). Under Products, add Sign In with LinkedIn using OpenID Connect (scopes openid, profile) and Share on LinkedIn (w_member_social). That is all a person needs to post as themselves. To post as a company page, request the Community Management API. Once LinkedIn approves it, the app may ask for r_organization_social, w_organization_social and rw_organization_admin.

data: For the administrator: what to set up so people can press Connect with Instagram under Settings › Integrations. Without it, the Instagram card says sign-in is not set up and accepts a pasted token instead.
data.in-pulse#In PULSE:
Set META_APP_ID and META_APP_SECRET (the secret from the instance’s secret store, never from a repository secret) and an https PULSE_PUBLIC_BASE_URL.
PULSE exchanges the sign-in for a long-lived token, stores it sealed, and renews it in its last ten days; a failed renewal is shown on the card. A permission the person did not grant is listed on the card, and a read that needs it says Reconnect to allow …. Disconnect removes PULSE’s grant at Meta (DELETE /me/permissions), then the stored tokens.
Connecting publishes nothing. Publishing also needs PULSE_APPLY_ENABLED and PULSE_PUBLISH_INSTAGRAM; replies need PULSE_PUBLISH_INSTAGRAM_REPLIES or PULSE_PUBLISH_INSTAGRAM_DMS. See Switches and arming order.
data.in-the-meta-developer-console#In the Met:
Create an app with Facebook Login for Business. PULSE uses the Instagram API with Facebook Login (Graph API v23.0): the person signs in at Facebook, and PULSE finds the Instagram professional account through the Facebook Page it is linked to.
Add /oauth/social/callback to the valid OAuth redirect URIs (see Public address and redirects).
Request these permissions. The sign-in asks for all of them at once:
