Permission Needed for instagram_basic, pages_show_list, pages_read_engagement Every feature instagram_content_publish Publishing posts, carousels, Reels and Stories instagram_manage_insights Results (reach, views, likes, comments, saves, shares) instagram_manage_comments Comments, replies, and posts that tag the account instagram_manage_messages, pages_manage_metadata Direct messages and replies to them Every permission needs Advanced Access through Meta App Review, and Meta asks for business verification, before it works for accounts that have no role on the app. Until then, only people with a role on the app can connect.
For direct messages, the Instagram account’s setting Allow access to messages must also be on.

data: For the administrator. Several connections send a person’s browser to a platform and back, and some platforms fetch files from PULSE. Both need the instance’s public address.
data.register-the-redirect-uris#Register the: Redirect URI Register it in Used by /oauth/social/callback the Meta app, the Google OAuth web client, the LinkedIn app Connect with Instagram, YouTube, LinkedIn /oauth/search-console/callback the Google OAuth web client Connect Search Console /oauth/mail/callback the Google OAuth web client, the Microsoft Entra app (Web platform) Connect Gmail, Connect Microsoft 365 Each must match exactly, including https and the absence of a trailing slash. A connect link works once and for ten minutes.
data.route-them-through-the-tide-edge#Route t: The callbacks are plain HTTP routes on the backend’s one port, like /media/ and /health. The TIDE edge that serves the PULSE host must pass /oauth/social/callback, /oauth/search-console/callback, /oauth/mail/callback, /media/, /podcast/feed.xml and the Twilio paths through to the backend unchanged. If a callback lands on the web app instead, the platform’s sign-in seems to succeed and the card stays not connected. See HTTP endpoints for the full list.
data.set-pulse_public_base_url#Set \u003ccode:
Set it on TIDE’s PulseControlPlane resource (or its overlay), never on the live Deployment, to the origin people use to open PULSE, for example https://pulse.example.com, with no trailing path.
It must be https. Over plain http PULSE does not offer Connect with Instagram, YouTube, LinkedIn or Search Console at all, because a sign-in code must never travel in clear text; the cards say what is missing.
The same address is used for:
the redirect URIs below; the signed, expiring /media/ links Instagram fetches photos, carousels and videos from (without it the Instagram channel is not ready); absolute links in the podcast feed (/podcast/feed.xml answers 503 without it); the Twilio callbacks (/comms/twilio/inbound, the AI-call routes); a trusted browser origin for the session cookie.

data:
For the administrator. PULSE has no speech engine of its own. Everything it says aloud goes to TIDE’s shared text-to-speech service, ttsd: the voiceover on Reels and Stories PULSE makes, read-back in the app, podcast and audiobook audio, and calls.
Setting Default Effect TTSD_URL http://ttsd.inference-system.svc.cluster.local:5005/v1/audio/speech (the in-cluster service) The full URL PULSE posts text to. Set it to an empty value to turn voice output off. TTSD_CALLER_KEY_FILE unset The file holding PULSE’s service key for ttsd. It is read on every call, so a rotated key needs no restart. With voice output off, or ttsd unreachable, a Reel or Story PULSE makes is a silent video that says “no voiceover: speech service unavailable”, and the features that need speech say it is unavailable instead of returning silence. Speech-to-text is separate: the voice tier at VOXTRAL_REMOTE_URL.
Making a video also needs ffmpeg on the server (the backend image has it; FFMPEG_PATH overrides the binary). Without it, the app says “video is not available on this server”.

The customer’s own website repository on GitHub. When a site audit finds something PULSE can fix in the site’s files, Propose as pull request opens one branch and one pull request there for a person to review and merge. PULSE never pushes to the base branch and never merges.
data.arm-proposals#Arm proposals: Proposing is off until the administrator sets both PULSE_APPLY_ENABLED=true and PULSE_AUDIT_APPLY=true, and only an administrator may propose. Either switch off refuses the proposal before anything is read from or sent to GitHub. PULSE_APPLY_ROOT is not needed. See Switches and arming order.
data.connect-it-in-pulse#Connect it in PULSE: An administrator opens Settings › Integrations › Website repository, enters the owner (user or organization), the repository name, the base branch (main when empty) and the token, and presses Connect and check. The token is sealed with the envelope key; leaving the field empty later keeps the stored one. The card shows one of: Connected, Missing permission, Token rejected, Base branch not found, GitHub unreachable, Not connected, with when it was last checked.
data.create-the-token-on-github#Create the to:
PULSE uses a fine-grained personal access token, not a GitHub OAuth app: an OAuth app’s narrowest write scope opens every repository the person can reach, while a fine-grained token can be limited to one.
On GitHub: Settings › Developer settings › Fine-grained tokens › Generate new token. Repository access: Only select repositories, and pick the site’s repository only. Permissions: Contents read and write, and Pull requests read and write. Nothing else. Choose an expiry you will remember to renew. No OAuth client and no server secret are needed for this connection.
data.what-a-proposal-does#What a proposal doe: Reads the base branch over the GitHub REST API, places the fix for one audit finding with the same stack logic as the server-side apply agent, and has the plan gate judge the edit against the measured finding. A dissent opens nothing and the proposal shows as withheld. Writes a new branch pulse/- and opens a pull request whose body cites the finding and the gate’s verdict. One proposal per finding. Never edits .github/workflows/ or .git/, refuses .. paths and links, and is capped at 20 files, 256 KiB each and 1 MiB in all. A fix already in the repository, or one that cannot be placed, is “No pull request needed” with the reason. The pull request’s state (open, merged, closed without merging) is read back from GitHub when asked. This is separate from the Website card, which publishes blog posts with the repository set in PULSE_SITE_REPO; see Site pipeline.

data.the-app-looks-empty#The app looks empty:
PULSE never fills a gap with an estimate. A figure it could not read is drawn as —, and a page with nothing behind it reads as empty rather than as a row of zeros. An empty page is usually a missing input, not a fault.
Brand Analysis says “No check-up yet”, and its cards say “Not checked yet”. Choose New site audit. See Getting started. Results read “Not measured”. Nothing measured the period yet. Connect Google Analytics, Google Ads or Search Console in Settings → Integrations. The work PULSE did is still counted, under What PULSE did. See Results and reports. “Results of your posts: not measured yet”. No platform reported results for your posts this week: connect Instagram, LinkedIn or YouTube, or wait for the first results after a post goes out. Campaigns has no drafts, and Leads has no tasks. Run a check-up. A finished check-up fills them. A card shows — where you expected a number. PULSE could not read that figure — usually a connection that is not set up, or a run that has not happened yet. Nothing is wrong with the card. See Measured and not measured.

data:
This guide follows the way you use Runink PULSE: Prescriptive Unified Lead & Social Engine, one page per step. You run a check-up of your business, act on what it found, approve the posts PULSE prepares, and then see what came of them.
1. Sign in and first check-upSign in, answer a few questions, and start your first check-up. 2. Brand AnalysisThe landing page: the cards, Needs you now, What PULSE did, and how you are doing over time. 3. The Brand Analysis pagesOne page per card: your plan, leads, competitors, search and AI, ideas, results. 4. LeadsFind, contact and follow up the people who could buy from you. 5. CampaignsThe board of posts, each campaign’s page, approving and scheduling, automations. 6. StudioMake content, read its checks, download it, publish it. 7. OpportunitiesPublic tenders and requests for proposals that need what you sell. 8. Results and reportsWhat was measured, what PULSE did, and PDF reports. 9. Connect your accountsSettings → Integrations: Instagram, YouTube, LinkedIn, Google, your website.
data.also-in-this-guide#Also in this guide: The site-score reportEvery check behind your site score, and its fixes as pull requests. Audit a domain in one lineType “Audit example.com” to the assistant: every stage of the check-up, and where each result goes. Website formSend your site’s contact-form enquiries straight to Leads. AI calls to leadsAn AI assistant calls a lead for you, within strict rules. Autopilot and agenciesPULSE posts what you approved at your best times; agencies run each client apart. Assistant and voiceAsk questions about your data and let the assistant propose actions. GlossaryThe words the app uses, in one list.
data.languages#Languages: The app ships in English, Spanish, French and Portuguese. Pick the language in Settings → Account. Content PULSE writes has its own language, set when it is made.
data.the-app-at-a-glance#The app at a glance:
The navigation rail on the left has two groups. On a phone it folds into a menu.
Group Pages Audience Brand Analysis (where PULSE opens), Leads (with Partners), Opportunities Content Campaigns, Studio At the foot of the rail is your account: the Settings gear and Sign out. Settings has the tabs Account, Integrations, Clients (for agencies) and Subscription. An administrator of your PULSE also reaches Admin from Settings → Account.
Every page has one title line. On its right is the bell, which lists what waits for you and what PULSE did recently. The same line shows your latest check-up: the site, whether it is still running and how it ended. Tap it to open the check-up on Brand Analysis.
The assistant floats in the bottom-right corner of every page. See Assistant and voice.

data:
An AI call is a phone call to one lead in which an AI assistant talks to the lead for you. It follows the lead’s drafted call script, works toward the goal you pick, and writes the outcome, a short summary and the next step to the lead when the call ends. It also creates a follow-up task.
Choose Call on a lead’s card, or AI call on its call-script draft. Automations can place the same call as a step.
data.outcomes#Outcomes: Outcome Follow-up task Meeting requested The next step the summary proposes Connected The next step the summary proposes Voicemail Call back in two days. With leave a short message, the assistant leaves one after the beep, starting with who is calling No answer Try again tomorrow Declined None: the number is on the do-not-call list Failed None The transcript is stored encrypted with the call. Only editors and administrators can read it. It is never written to the server log.
data.what-the-call-says#What the call says: “Hello, this is an AI assistant calling on behalf of your company.” The recording notice: “This call is recorded and transcribed for control and quality purposes.” The first sentence of the drafted script, then the conversation. If the lead says stop, do not call (or the same in French, Spanish or Portuguese), the assistant says goodbye, the number goes on your do-not-call list, and the call is marked Declined. The model is not asked.
data.when-pulse-refuses-to-call#When PULSE re:
The server checks every call. It refuses, and lists every reason, when:
an administrator has not armed AI calls (PULSE_APPLY_ENABLED, PULSE_OUTBOUND_CALLS and PULSE_AI_CALLS, see Switches); you are a viewer (AI calls need an editor or administrator); there is no record of the lead’s prior express consent to AI calls for their current number. An AI voice is an artificial voice under the US Telephone Consumer Protection Act (FCC ruling, February 2024). Record how the lead agreed (web form, written agreement, recorded call, other), where the evidence is, and when; the number is on the do-not-call list; the lead’s time zone is not set, or it is outside the calling hours in the lead’s local time. Calling hours never extend before 08:00 or after 21:00 local time; the lead already had the chosen number of AI calls (at most three) in the last 30 days, or a call to them is still in progress; the lead has no drafted call script, Twilio has no caller number, or speech is not configured. Check runs the same checks without calling.

data.ask-about-your-data-and-let-it-propose-a:
The assistant can read your own PULSE records to answer: your leads (by stage) and one lead’s details, your latest audit and its findings, your metrics (when nothing has been measured yet it says so instead of giving 0), content waiting for your approval, your campaigns, and follow-up tasks that are due. While it reads, the chat shows what it is doing (“Reading your leads…”). Each read is also listed on your activity card.
It can also propose an action: start an audit, find leads, draft outreach for a lead, move a lead’s stage, create a campaign draft, write a Studio whitepaper or presentation outline, approve or schedule a content item. A proposal appears as a card that says what it will do and on which page. Nothing runs until you tap Confirm. Confirm is checked again on the server: your role must still allow the action, and the card’s details cannot be changed from the app. A card expires after 15 minutes.
The assistant never sends an email, posts or calls by itself. Approving or scheduling a content item goes through the same publishing switches as the Campaigns board’s own buttons.
Every read and every action is done with your account: the assistant cannot do anything you could not do by tapping. It reads or proposes at most four times per question.
data.ask-it-to-audit-a-site#Ask it to audit a:
One line with a verb and a web address — Audit example.com — starts the whole audit: PULSE reads the site, scores it, writes the diagnosis, and fills the pages that act on it, stage by stage. The verbs it recognizes are audit, analyse (or analyze), scan, review, inspect, and score. A line with a question mark is treated as a question instead. See Audit a domain.
A web address whose host is not a domain runs the site relevance audit on its own and opens the full report.
data.talk-instead-of-typing#Talk instead of t: Voice input. The microphone records a clip and uploads it to /voice/transcribe. Speech-to-text runs on the platform’s own Voxtral server, and is available only where a deployment has configured a voice tier; otherwise it answers that it is unavailable rather than returning an empty transcript. Spoken replies. The assistant can read answers aloud through ModelService.SynthesizeSpeech. Speech is synthesized by Runink TIDE’s shared ttsd service — PULSE embeds no speech engine of its own. Where a deployment has turned voice output off, the reply stays text. Both voice endpoints require you to be signed in.
data.the-assistant#The assistant:
The assistant floats over every screen, and it is told which screen you are on. It sends your messages to ModelService.Complete with the assistant agent and streams the answer back.
Everything it says comes from the platform’s own model. Nothing goes to an outside AI service.
data.voice-calls-with-the-assistant#Voice cal:
The full-screen call view (/call) negotiates a WebRTC call through /voice/webrtc/offer. PULSE only relays the signaling. The call itself is carried by the platform’s shared calling agent, which the deployment names in CALLING_AGENT_URL. When that is not set, the offer is refused with HTTP 503 rather than connecting a call that carries no audio.
Phone calls to leads are different. See AI calls to leads.

data:
Runink PULSE: Prescriptive Unified Lead & Social Engine can fill most of its pages from one sentence. Type Audit and a web address into the assistant, and PULSE reads the site, scores it, writes the diagnosis, and copies the result into the pages that act on it. You do not have to know what else to ask for.
Each stage on the way is tracked. A stage that wrote something says where its result came from. A stage that could not finish says why, and the pages it would have filled stay empty rather than showing something made up.
data.attach-your-own-material#Attach your own:
The new-audit form also takes photos or a short video of your store or product, product documents and voice notes, so the audit compares your site against them: what the material shows that the site does not say, where the two disagree, and which benefits the site never communicates.
Kind Accepted Limits What PULSE reads Photo JPEG, PNG, WebP (not HEIC: share it as JPEG) 15 MB A description and the visible text, from the platform’s vision tier Video MP4, MOV, WebM 60 MB, 60 seconds Four frames, each described like a photo Document PDF, DOCX (50 pages, 20 MB); TXT, MD (2 MB) The text. A scanned PDF has none; text recognition is not run Voice note WAV, WebM, OGG, M4A, MP3 20 MB, 5 minutes A transcript, from the same voice tier as the microphone Each file is sealed in PULSE’s encrypted store as it arrives; it is never kept as a plain file. Only you can see your attachments. One that no audit used is removed after 24 hours; one an audit used is removed 30 days after that audit started. You can delete one at any time.
When something cannot be read, the attachment says so, and the audit does not use it: image understanding unavailable (this deployment has no vision tier), frames not analysed, transcription unavailable, or no text found. PULSE never describes a photo it could not look at.
The Your attached material stage on the card lists what the diagnosis was given. Findings that come from the material name the attachment they come from, and are reviewed like every other part of the plan.
If an audit of the same domain is already running, a new audit with attachments the running one was not started with is refused with an audit of example.com is already running, rather than joining it without them. Your attachments are kept: run the audit again when the current one finishes.
data.content-ideas-for-your-customers-deep-re:
At the end of a check-up PULSE turns what it measured into content ideas, shown on Brand Analysis. Each idea is a scenario: one kind of customer, one problem they have, one angle (teach, show proof, behind the scenes, offer, event), and the Instagram or YouTube formats it suits, with 3 to 5 post ideas and the findings that back it.
What it sells first. The offerings stage lists what your site says you sell, each with the site’s own words; a row whose words are not on the page is dropped. Ideas and content-gap cards are tied to one of these. A gap that serves nothing you sell is kept off the cards. What people search for. With Google Search Console connected, the searches people type before they find your site, and where your site ranks for them, are the first measured demand an idea can cite. Who it is for comes from what you told PULSE, the leads the audit found, or the diagnosis’s audience. PULSE never invents a customer. See Personas. Each scenario is checked: PULSE’s own web research, its checks on the ideas (3 to 5, the right formats, about what you sell, nothing you asked to avoid), the guardrails and the plan gate. Ideas that do not pass are listed as held back, with the reason. So are scenarios the time budget could not pay for. Your Instagram week: a 7-day plan across several scenarios, never the same topic two days running and at most one offer post in any four. Tune (on the card, or Fine-tune the content ideas before a check-up) sets who you sell to, what you sell, where you post, how often, topics to focus on or avoid, language, region and depth. Quick is the default; Deep asks PULSE’s model to think each idea through first and takes longer. Saving on an existing check-up makes new ideas from the same findings.
data.how-long-it-takes#How long it takes:
Minutes. Most stages are model calls, and they run one after another on the CPU inference tier. When another audit is running on the same deployment, your stages wait their turn, and the card shows Waiting for the model (position N in the queue).
You can leave the page. The audit keeps running on the server, and each page fills in as its stage finishes. When you come back to the assistant, the card reconnects to the run.
While it runs, the title line of every page follows it: the domain, whether it is still running and how it ended, and the reason the run gives. Tapping it opens the check-up on Brand Analysis.
data.how-the-audit-ends#How the audit ends: Card heading Meaning Done — every page was populated Every stage is done. The publishing schedule may be skipped. Partly done — some pages are still empty (see the failed stages) Some stages finished and some did not. The failed and blocked stages are listed with their reasons. The audit failed No stage that fills a page finished.
data.resume-run-again-or-reuse#Resume, run ag: Resume the audit runs it again from the first stage that is not done. Stages already done on the same input are not repeated, and nothing they wrote is written twice. Run it again starts a fresh audit even if one finished recently. Asking again within 24 hours of a finished audit returns that audit as it is, with a note saying when it ran. Use Run it again to force a new one. Asking while an audit of the same domain is already running joins it. The card says Joined the audit already running for this domain and replays every stage from the start. A fresh run never switches the campaign to active: it updates the one campaign it keeps for this domain and leaves its status alone. It never deletes or changes drafts that earlier runs left in Drafts to approve.
data.start-over#Start over: Settings › Account and the check-up history on Brand Analysis have Start over: type your domain to delete every check-up of this account (or agency client) and what it made: findings, content ideas, campaign suggestions you did not accept, drafts you did not approve. You can also tick accepted campaigns, the leads check-ups found, and approved or scheduled posts not sent yet. Anything published, its measured results and your connected accounts are never deleted. It is refused while a check-up is running.
data.the-stages#The stages:
The card lists every stage of the audit as it runs, under the heading Running — each page fills in as its stage finishes.
Step on the card What it does Where the result goes Domain Normalizes what you typed into the domain and the address to read. — Read the site, Site score, Search trends Reads your live site, scores it, and looks up search interest in your business. Brand Analysis › Can people find you?, and the site fixes in Your plan Google Discover readiness Checks Google’s Discover requirements on your live page: HTTPS, mobile viewport, large image previews, a share image of at least 1200 px, article schema and a publication date. Discover traffic itself is only in Search Console. Brand Analysis › Ready for Google Discover Retention signals Looks for what your site offers existing customers: sign-in, docs, support, changelog, community, newsletter, blog. Churn itself needs customer data. Brand Analysis › Customers you might lose Your attached material Gives the diagnosis what your attachments contain, labelled as material you provided. Skipped when nothing was attached. Your material on Brand Analysis, with the findings drawn from each file Diagnosis Writes the diagnosis of your market position and a plan. The plan is reviewed before anything is saved. Brand Analysis Follow-up plan Turns the plan into a 30-day cycle of tasks. Brand Analysis › Your plan, and To do today on Leads Drafts for approval One draft per suggestion in the channel plan. Campaigns, column Drafts to approve Campaign One campaign for this domain, linked to the diagnosis. Campaigns Publishing schedule Puts the plan’s dates on its drafts. Nothing is queued until you approve a draft; approving it while its date is still ahead schedules it then. Campaigns (the date shows on each draft) Creatives One creative brief per suggested piece. Briefs, not finished media. Studio › My Library Course One draft course built from the plan. Studio › My Library (Learning) Market summary The diagnosis’s positioning and competitive sections. Brand Analysis › What people are talking about Niche The niche the rest of the research is about. When the diagnosis did not finish, it is read from your site’s own text instead, and the stage says so. — Trending posts, Competitor channels, Guest opportunities, Leads Research on the web for your niche. Each lead found gets a fit tier (high, medium, low) from what its record holds; it is not a probability. Every lead lands in New with the contact its page publishes and where it was found, and is listed under Brand Analysis › People who could buy from you. Brand Analysis (What people are talking about, Who you compete with, Partners to contact, People who could buy from you) and Leads What you sell, Content ideas What your site says you sell, quoted word for word, then the content ideas built on it. See below. Brand Analysis › How your business comes across and Ideas for what to post Visibility in GenAI answers Measured by search only; no AI assistant is queried. Access: robots.txt is read for 11 AI crawlers (GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, ClaudeBot, Claude-SearchBot, PerplexityBot, Google-Extended, Applebot-Extended, CCBot, Bytespider, meta-externalagent), plus /llms.txt, how much of the home page’s text is in the raw HTML, and JSON-LD in that raw HTML — each pass/fail with the line that decided it. Answers: for up to 8 buyer questions built from your niche, audience, brand and competitors, a search engine’s own result page is rendered and read for an AI answer — Brave Search’s AI answer, Bing’s Copilot answer, Google’s AI Overview or DuckDuckGo’s Search Assist, trying them in that order and skipping any engine that is refusing PULSE’s address: whether it shows one, the sources it cites, whether your domain and which competitors are among them, and your organic rank. Each answer names the engine it was read from. A page that did not load is not measured, never not cited. Not read: chat assistants. Fixes (robots.txt, llms.txt, structured data) are in the site score’s actions. Brand Analysis › Can people find you? Content gaps Where your content under-serves demand, by topic and format, with a coverage index. Each gap cites the audit findings it is drawn from (E1, E2 …: the site score and its weakest checks, missing Google Discover requirements and retention surfaces, trend searches, GenAI visibility); its demand, coverage and opportunity scores are the model’s estimates. From the gaps that cite a finding, PULSE proposes one campaign whose objective matches your first goal that names one (sales, lead generation, brand awareness or engagement). Brand Analysis › Ideas for what to post, and the proposal on Campaigns Competitors and where you win Possible competitors: the ones you named, the sites search engines show instead of yours for buyer questions (from the GenAI-visibility result pages), and competitor channels a search confirmed. For each with a website (up to four), the same checks run on both home pages (Google Discover requirements, retention surfaces): where you win and where you lose. A site that cannot be read is not measured, never a loss. Brand Analysis › Who you compete with, Where you win and where you lose Partner contacts Each partner found — the guest opportunities, plus its own search for complementary businesses, associations and newsletters in your niche, so it does not depend on the guest search — with the email, phone and LinkedIn its own page publishes, read by the crawler. A partner no search confirmed and whose page does not answer is not listed. Brand Analysis › Partners to contact New customer groups to try Up to five niches next to yours. The model proposes them from search results it must cite; one that cites nothing is dropped, and the plan gate judges the rest (withheld ones are not shown). Brand Analysis › New groups of customers to try Every figure in the stages from Follow-up plan to Market summary comes from the diagnosis; none is invented along the way.
Guest opportunities whose address the search actually returned are kept with their source and a Relevance (search fit) score, never a follower figure. They show under Brand Analysis › Partners to contact. See The Brand Analysis pages.
data.what-each-status-means#What each status: Status Meaning done The stage wrote at least one row, or a source that really answered found nothing. The row shows where the result came from: sourced from the web, inferred by the model, or sourced and inferred, plus the first source address. failed The stage ran and could not write anything, or had nothing to work from. The row gives the reason, for example had 4 to write, wrote 0 or no trend search answered (0 of 3 queries). The page it feeds stays empty. skipped The stage did not run. Either it was blocked because a stage it depends on did not finish (the reason starts with blocked:), or it is the publishing schedule and every channel it would queue on is switched off. waiting The stage is in the queue for the model, at the position shown. A finding of “0” counts as done only when the source answered. When no search answered at all, the stage is failed: silence is not reported as an empty result.
data.what-is-never-inferred#What is never inf:
The audit writes no performance numbers.
Results are not filled by an audit. Impressions, clicks, conversions, and return come only from the accounts you connect. Partners and shows found by an audit carry no follower, audience, or engagement figure. Their score measures how well the show fits your niche, and the label says so. Audience sizes on the market pages are shown only when the search results stated them. An unknown size stays unknown; it is never estimated. The site score comes from deterministic checks on the live site. Checks that need a data source you have not connected are left out and listed, not counted as zero.
data.what-you-type#What you type:
Open the assistant and send one line with a verb and a domain:
Audit example.com The verbs PULSE recognizes are audit, analyse (or analyze), scan, review, inspect, and score. A full address such as https://example.com/pricing works too; PULSE keeps only the host name, lower-cased.
A line that contains a question mark is treated as a question and goes to the model as an ordinary chat turn. To run the audit, leave the question mark out. An IP address or localhost is refused with "…" is not a domain (expected something like example.com). Running an audit needs the editor or admin role. A viewer can read the result but not start one. See What each role may call. The reply is a card titled Audit of example.com, with one row per stage.
data.where-to-see-past-audits#Where to see pa:
Every audit, with its stages and their reasons, is kept per user. AuditPipelineService/ListAuditRuns lists yours, newest first, and GetAuditRun returns one. See the API reference.
On Brand Analysis, Your check-ups lists them with their date, how many parts finished and their status. Tap one and the whole page shows it; the latest is shown by default. Delete one, or Clear all previous check-ups (type the domain to confirm; the latest stays unless you tick it). Deleting removes the check-up’s steps, what it found and its AI-visibility results; your leads, campaigns, drafts and site-score history stay.
data.why-publishing-schedule-says-skipped#Why:
The schedule stage puts each planned date on a draft of the same channel. It queues nothing: a post waits for your approval, and approving a draft while its date is still ahead schedules it for that date (on a channel that is switched on). When the plan has no draft to put a date on, the stage ends skipped with no draft to put the plan's times on; the tasks are on the Planner (the tasks are in Brand Analysis › Your plan). That is not a fault and does not make the audit partial.
A post whose date passes while it is still waiting for approval is marked missed with the reason, and is never sent late: reschedule it from the Scheduled column on Campaigns.

data: PULSE is your marketing agency in an app. You approve the posts; PULSE does the rest of the work an agency would: it posts them at the right time, keeps an eye on the comments, and tells you every week what it did and what came of it. Agencies use the same app to run all their clients, each in its own space.
data.autopilot-pulse-runs-the-account-after-y:
Turn it on per account under Settings › Integrations › Autopilot. With Autopilot on:
Approving a post queues it at the account’s best time instead of sending it at once. Nothing you have not approved is ever queued. Best time comes from your own posts: once 8 of them have results, PULSE ranks the days and hours that got the most reactions and comments. Until then the card says PULSE’s starting schedule, not measured yet (for LinkedIn: weekday mornings and lunchtime). How often follows your campaign board (the number of pieces planned for that week on that channel). You can set your own pace instead, or go back to the board. Every send is recorded, with what happened: posted, held back by a switch, or failed with the platform’s reason (on the post’s step trail, and under Recent dispatches on its Integrations card). A short outage is retried after 5, 20 and 80 minutes. It stops by itself when the connection expires, when the platform asks PULSE to slow down, or after three failed posts in a row. Leads › To do today then says so in plain words with a Reconnect link. Resume moves the posts that waited to the next good times, so nothing goes out in a burst. Pause and Resume are one tap. Turning Autopilot off cancels its queued posts; the content stays approved. The server’s publishing switches still have the last word: if your administrator has switched publishing off, Autopilot posts nothing and the card says so. See Switches and arming order.
data.comments-and-replies#Comments and replie:
On LinkedIn, Instagram and YouTube, each new comment on a post PULSE published gets a drafted reply under Replies waiting for you on Campaigns (Needs you now on Brand Analysis counts them). Edit it, send it, or dismiss it. On Instagram, posts that tag your account (mentions) and direct messages land there too, each marked as a comment, a mention or a message. A message can be answered only within 24 hours of the person’s last message; after that PULSE says so and sends nothing. YouTube has no mentions or direct messages, and the app says “not available on YouTube”. If the connection lacks a permission, the account says Reconnect to allow … (see Connect your accounts). PULSE never makes comments up.
Answer simple comments by itself is off until you turn it on, and then covers only:
a thank-you to a kind comment, an answer taken from FAQ content you approved, your opening hours or a link to your own website. Even then the reply goes out only after PULSE’s safety rules (OpenBias) and its plan check both agree; otherwise it waits for you. Everything else, a complaint, a price question, an order, always waits for you.
data.for-agencies-one-space-per-client#For ag:
Under Settings › Clients, add each client business. Each client has its own brand, accounts, Autopilot, approvals and reports, and one client never sees another client’s data. Switch between your own business and your clients from the business switcher at the top right of every page.
Give people a role on each client:
Agency admin: runs everything for that client and adds people. Client approver: sees the work and approves or rejects posts and replies. Nothing else. Use this for the client’s owner. Everyone you add must already use this PULSE; billing stays per seat.
Not yet: billing per client, a white-label report, and per-client HubSpot and GitHub connections (those stay on each person’s own account).
data.what-pulse-did-this-week#What PULSE did,: In What PULSE did on Brand Analysis, This week shows: posts published, replies sent (and how many PULSE sent on its own), the reactions, comments and views the platforms reported, and what is queued next. A figure no platform reported is shown as not measured, never as 0. Email me this sends it to you from your own connected mailbox.

data:
Each card on Brand Analysis opens its own page (/brand-analysis?section=…). Every page names the check-up it reads and its date, with a way to pick another check-up, and lists everything that check-up kept, not just the preview on the card. Before your first check-up, a page says so and offers to start one.
A page never fills a gap with a guess. It tells apart four cases: found, nothing found (the source answered and had nothing), Not measured in this check-up, and could not be read right now.
data.how-people-see-you#How people see you: Can people find you? (?section=searchAi): Your site score and its parts; Can AI tools read your site (your robots.txt for AI crawlers, /llms.txt, text and structured data in the raw page); What AI answers say when buyers ask (for buyer questions, whether a search engine’s AI answer cites you and which competitors it cites, and your rank); Where you show up in search results; and, once you connect Google Search Console, Google searches (Search Console): clicks and appearances in the last 28 days against the 28 before, your Top searches, searches Close to the first page (average position 4 to 15) and Pages losing clicks. Without Search Console it says Not measured and links to Integrations. What people are talking about (?section=market): what the market research measured and every trending post it saved, with its picture only when one loads. A heat score is labelled as the model’s estimate. How your business comes across (?section=brand): Who buys from you and What you sell, each marked with where it came from: your own answers, your site, your leads, or the analysis. Ready for Google Discover (?section=discover): which of Google’s Discover requirements your live page meets (HTTPS, mobile layout, large image previews, a share image of at least 1200 px, article markup, a publication date). Discover traffic itself is only in Search Console.
data.ideas-for-what-to-post#Ideas for what to:
Ideas for what to post (?section=ideas): first the topics your customers look for that your site does not cover (content gaps), then the content ideas: for one kind of customer, one problem and one angle, three to five post ideas and the findings behind them. Ideas that did not pass PULSE’s checks are listed as held back, with the reason. How they are made: Content ideas.
From the content gaps, PULSE may propose a campaign; it waits on Campaigns.
data.old-addresses#Old addresses: The pages that used to be the Site Audit result, its history, the Market Radar, the Persona Profile and Influencers now open here or on Leads: /site-audit/result opens Brand Analysis, /site-audit/history opens Your check-ups, /market opens What people are talking about, and /partners and /influencers open Leads → Partners.
data.results#Results: Results (?section=results): your measured figures for the period and their impact. See Results and reports. Your last check-up (?section=checkup): when it ran, how it went, and every stage with what it did or why it did not, plus your other check-ups. See how this was done (/site-audit/log) has the full log.
data.your-leads#Your leads: People who could buy from you (?section=leads): every lead the check-up found, with the contact its page publishes and where it was found. Each has a fit tier (high, medium, low) read from what its record holds; it is not a probability. The leads are on Leads in New. How likely your leads are to buy (?section=conversion) and Customers you might lose (?section=churn): what that research area of the check-up read, its status and a note, and where to act on it. Customers you might lose is read from what your site offers existing customers (sign-in, docs, support, newsletter …); churn itself needs customer data.
data.your-market#Your market: Who you compete with (?section=competitors): the competitors the check-up named (the ones you gave, the sites search engines show instead of yours, and channels a search confirmed), with their channels. Where you win and where you lose (?section=edge): the same checks run on your home page and each competitor’s. A site that could not be read is not measured, never a loss. Partners to contact (?section=partners): businesses, associations, newsletters and shows the check-up found, with the email, phone or LinkedIn their own page publishes, and the shows and channels you could appear on. The same partners are on Leads → Partners. New groups of customers to try (?section=niches): up to five niches next to yours, each backed by the search results it cites. One that cites nothing is dropped, and the plan gate withholds the ones it disagrees with.
data.your-plan#Your plan:
Your plan: fixes for your site and posts (?section=plan).
Fixes for your site: what the site score found, highest impact first. Your 30-day plan: the follow-up cycle the check-up made from its plan: the week you are in, Tasks, week by week, a Calendar by channel, and Where you started and where you are, which is measured only from your weekly check-ins (you add them on Leads). The open tasks are what Needs you now counts as “things to do”.
The full list of checks and fixes is the site-score report. To have PULSE propose a site fix as a pull request on your own website repository, see Website repository.

data:
Brand Analysis (/brand-analysis) is where PULSE opens: how your business looks online, what PULSE did for you, and what to do next. It reads your latest check-up and the accounts you connected. It shows only what was measured; a figure nobody measured says Not measured, never 0.
At the top are New site audit (starts a check-up, see Sign in and first check-up) and View History (your check-ups).
data.further-down-the-page#Further down the p: Below the overview are Content ideas for your customers (see Ideas for what to post), short previews of what the check-up found about leads, competitors, partners and new groups of customers, and one collapsed card per research area that has something to show.
data.how-you-are-doing-over-time#How you are:
How you are doing over time draws a line only for what has measured points in the chosen days, and a line starts once there are two.
Line Source Site score over time · Named in AI answers over time · Searches where you appear · Google Discover ready Your check-ups, one point each Engaged visits · Page views Google Analytics Ad views · Ad clicks Google Ads Search clicks · Search impressions Google Search Console People who saw your posts What LinkedIn and Instagram reported for your posts What was never measured is listed on one line (Not measured yet: …), what is connected but has no measured day yet on another, and each source you have not connected gets one Connect button.
data.the-cards#The cards:
Below the buttons, every part of Brand Analysis is a card, grouped in the order you act on them. Each card gives its one-line answer from the check-up and a dot:
Measured: PULSE has a real answer (it may be “nothing found”). Not measured: the check-up did not measure it, is still running, or that part did not finish. Needs a connection: only a connected account can answer it (for Results, Google Analytics or Google Ads). Group Cards Your plan Your plan: fixes for your site and posts Your leads People who could buy from you · How likely your leads are to buy · Customers you might lose Your market Who you compete with · Where you win and where you lose · Partners to contact · New groups of customers to try How people see you Can people find you? · What people are talking about · How your business comes across · Ready for Google Discover Ideas Ideas for what to post Results Results · Your last check-up Tap a card to open its page. Every page says which check-up it shows and when it ran, and Brand Analysis takes you back. See The Brand Analysis pages.
data.the-key-numbers#The key numbers:
One period selector, 7 / 30 / 90 days, sets the numbers below it. Each number shows its change when the earlier period was measured too.
Number Where it comes from Site score The check-up’s score of your site, out of 100 New leads found Leads PULSE found in the period, counted from its own records; tap it to open Leads Named in AI answers Of the AI answers the check-up read on search engines, how many cited your site (“N of M”) Times people saw you Impressions your connected accounts reported in the period Site score and Named in AI answers appear only once there is a check-up; Times people saw you needs a connected source.
data.what-pulse-did#What PULSE did:
What PULSE did is counted from what PULSE itself saved, so a 0 here is a real 0, marked Counted. Nothing in it is estimated.
Posts published, per channel, drafts approved, outreach messages drafted, follow-up tasks done, and leads contacted or moved on. This week: replies sent (and how many PULSE sent on its own), the results of your posts that the platforms reported, and what goes out next. A result no platform reported says Results of your posts: not measured yet. Email me this sends the week to you from your own connected mailbox. Results measured: impressions, clicks, conversions, engagement and ad spend for the period, with engagement by channel, from what your connected accounts reported, and on how many days of the period they were measured. Without them it says Not measured and offers Open Integrations. Something PULSE keeps no record of says not recorded. For example, a post sent at the moment you approve it is not yet counted here, and the card says so.
data.what-this-check-up-measured-and-your-che: What this check-up measured draws your site score as a gauge and every dimension the check-up scored, each out of 100. Grey means not measured, not zero. Your check-ups appears once you have more than one. Tap a check-up to see the whole page as it was then. You can delete one, or Clear all previous check-ups (type your domain to confirm; the latest stays unless you tick it). Deleting removes the check-up’s steps, what it found and its AI visibility results; your leads, campaigns, drafts and site-score history stay. Start over removes every check-up and what it made; see Start over. Your material lists each file you gave the check-up as A1, A2 …, with every finding that cites it.
data.your-last-check-up-and-needs-you-now#You:
Side by side on a wide screen, one above the other on a phone:
Your last check-up: the site and when it was checked, then either Everything was checked. or how many parts finished (the rest are tried again on the next check-up). See how this was done opens every stage, where each answer came from and the full text of anything that failed. Check again starts a new check-up. Before the first one, this is where it says No check-up yet.
Needs you now: one line and one button per thing waiting for you:
Your plan: N things to do, with See all; N drafts wait for your review, with Review (opens the drafts on Campaigns); N replies wait for you, with Review (the replies Autopilot drafted). When all three were read and none waits, it says Nothing waits for you right now. If one could not be read, it says so rather than claiming there is nothing.
When you look at an earlier check-up, a line above says Showing the check-up of its date, with Show the latest.

data:
Campaigns (/campaigns) is where posts are planned, approved, scheduled and followed until they go out. It is one page, built like Leads: what needs you, a few counts, your campaigns, then one board of every post.
Every card on the board is one post, never a whole campaign. How a post moves from idea to sent is explained in Drafts, approval and publishing.
data.a-campaigns-own-page#A campaign\u0026rsq:
Open campaign opens /campaigns/. All campaigns takes you back.
At the top:
its state (Not started, Running, Paused, Finished, Archived), its dates, budget, spend and channels, with Edit Campaign and Start, Pause or Resume. A running campaign gets PULSE’s daily drafts; a paused one does not. Spend is shown only when an ad account reports it; Why PULSE proposed it, for a campaign PULSE proposed; its phases, one line each: name, weeks, and how many of its posts are made; its milestones, each with its done criteria and who approves it; Results: the plan’s targets with what was measured against them. A result PULSE has not measured says so, never 0. Without a plan it says No targets yet. Below, Board shows the same board narrowed to this campaign, and Timeline shows every recorded step of every post in date order. Steps with no recorded time are counted, not placed.
data.approve-and-schedule#Approve and schedul:
Move a draft to Scheduled to approve it and schedule it in one step: PULSE asks for the day and time. Approve from Needs you now approves it without a time. With Autopilot on for that account, PULSE then queues it at the account’s best time. With Autopilot off, it goes out when you approve it, or at its planned time if it already has one that is still ahead. Move a scheduled post to Scheduled again to pick a new time. Some moves are refused, with the reason:
A post that is only an idea cannot be scheduled: Write it first. Nothing moves to Sent by hand. A post reaches Sent only when it really went out. A written post never goes back to Planned. Approving does not by itself publish. Whether a post goes out is decided when it is due: its channel must be connected and Active, and your administrator must have publishing switched on. Otherwise the post stays in Scheduled marked held back (withheld) or failed, with the reason. A post whose time passed while it waited for approval is marked missed and is never sent late; reschedule it or remove it.
data.automate#Automate:
Every card (posts, leads, partners, opportunities) has Automate. It opens that item’s own automation over the page: a trigger, then steps. Tap a step to change it; add or remove steps. The assistant can propose steps; you approve them.
An automation is disarmed until you arm it: then it runs only as a Dry run, which shows what it would do. Once armed, it runs by itself when its trigger fires, and anything it sends still needs the server’s publishing switches. A step the server cannot carry out says so, and an automation that cannot run yet lists why.
data.campaigns-pulse-proposes#Campaigns PULSE:
From a check-up’s content gaps, PULSE may propose a campaign whose objective matches your goal. It waits under What your audit found and in the strip as Proposed by PULSE:
Review and accept shows the proposal; you can change its name, objective (required) and description, then accept it. Accepting prepares its content strategy and plan. Nothing is published. Dismiss sets it aside. Set-aside proposals are kept, and you can open one again and accept it.
data.make-its-plan#Make its plan:
A campaign without a plan offers Make its plan (Change the plan once it has one). Plan your calendar asks what you can manage:
the first and last day, and an event if there is one (its day and how many days it lasts); how many posts a week you can manage per channel, and Instagram Stories a day during the event; how often a post sells something (One post in every N sells something). PULSE lays the posts out inside that. It places each post at your best time where it has measured one (otherwise at a starting time it labels as such), and writes a first idea for each post: topic, format, who it is for, first line and what readers should do, plus a tone for each persona and three results to aim for. Its checks test your capacity, the selling ratio, the dates and duplicates, and the plan gate reviews the plan against your check-up. Writing it can take a few minutes; you can leave the page.
PULSE needs to know who you talk to. If no check-up or lead tells it, the plan is refused with: PULSE does not know who you talk to yet: run a site audit (it asks who buys from you) or add leads, then plan again.
The plan’s posts appear in Planned. Studio writes them, and Autopilot never queues a post before its planned time.
data.old-addresses#Old addresses: /approval, /publishing, /strategy, /content-strategy, /content-gaps, /strategy-roadmap and /automations open this page; /approval and /publishing bring Drafts to approve into view.
data.the-board#The board:
Four columns, in order:
Column What is in it Planned Posts a campaign’s plan holds that are not written yet. Create opens Studio to write one. Drafts to approve Written posts waiting for your OK. Each says when it is planned for, or Not scheduled, and its next step. Scheduled Approved posts with a time to go out (Goes out …), or Approved: pick a time to send it. A post that did not go out stays here with its reason. Sent Posts that went out, with the day. A card names its channel and where it came from: its campaign, From your check-up of …, Placed by Autopilot, or Not in a campaign. Open a card to read the post, its steps and its actions:
Draft opens it in Studio to write or change it. Download saves it as files you can post yourself (approved, scheduled and sent posts). See Download. Move moves it to another column (see the rules below). Discard (drafts) rejects it. A rejected post leaves the board. Reschedule and Remove (scheduled posts). Automate opens its own automation. See Automate.
data.the-campaign-strip#The campaign strip:
One row per campaign, newest first (archived ones and proposals you set aside are left out). Each row shows its state and its counts: N planned · N to approve · N scheduled · N sent. Why shows why PULSE proposed it.
Tap a campaign to narrow the board to its posts. Open campaign opens its own page. A campaign PULSE proposed and you have not accepted is read only, marked Proposed by PULSE, with Review and accept and Dismiss. While its plan is being prepared it says Preparing its plan, then Plan ready (or Plan failed).
data.the-step-trail#The step trail:
Open any card, or use Timeline, to see Its steps:
Planned → Drafted → Approved → Scheduled → Sent, or Withheld, Failed or Missed.
Each step says when it happened and what PULSE recorded: the phase and planned date, which skill wrote the draft and its check results, who approved it, when it was queued and for when, and where it went out or why it did not. Every step is read from what PULSE stored:
not yet: the step has not happened; not recorded: it happened (a later step proves it) but PULSE kept no record of it, for example who approved a post approved before approvals were recorded. A post sent through a channel you have not connected says to download it and post it yourself, rather than showing the platform’s raw error.
data.the-top-of-the-page#The top of the page: Needs you now: each post that waits for you, one line each: Approve “…”, Write “…” (a post that is still only an idea), or "…" did not go out with the reason. Do it acts on it; Skip puts it off until your next visit. When nothing waits it says Nothing waits for you. The counts: Running campaigns, Proposals waiting, Drafts to approve, Scheduled this week, Sent this week. A count PULSE could not read shows —, never 0. Replies waiting for you: the replies Autopilot drafted to comments, mentions and messages. See Autopilot. What your audit found: the campaigns PULSE proposes. See below. Two buttons float at the bottom right: New Campaign, and Check a competitor’s content, which compares what a competitor publishes with yours.

data:
The words the app uses, in alphabetical order.
Word Meaning Active Your switch on a channel’s card in Settings → Integrations. An Active channel gets PULSE’s daily drafts, is planned in campaigns, and may publish. Approve Your OK on a draft. It hands the post to the schedule; it does not by itself publish. See Drafts, approval and publishing. Armed / disarmed An automation is disarmed until you arm it: until then it runs only as a dry run. Your administrator’s publishing switches are armed or disarmed in the same sense. Automate The button on every card that opens that item’s own automation: a trigger, then steps. Autopilot PULSE posting what you approved at each account’s best time, and drafting replies to comments. Per account, in Settings → Integrations. Best time When your posts get the most reactions and comments, measured from your own posts once enough of them have results. Until then PULSE uses a starting schedule and says so. Brand Analysis The landing page: your check-up, what PULSE did, and your results. Campaign A goal with dates, channels and a plan of posts. Its own page is /campaigns/. Check-up One run of PULSE over your website and the web: site score, AI and search visibility, leads, competitors, partners, content ideas. Also called a site audit. Checks The tests PULSE runs on a draft it wrote (opening line, caption, slides, hashtags …): passed, needs work, or could not be checked. Content ideas Post ideas for one kind of customer, one problem and one angle, backed by what the check-up measured. Counted A figure from PULSE’s own records. A 0 that is counted is a real 0. Draft A written post waiting for your approval (column Drafts to approve). Also the button that writes a message to a lead. Dry run Running an automation to see what it would do, without doing it. Held back (withheld) A post, reply or proposal that was stopped on purpose: by a publishing switch, a missing connection, or the plan gate. It is never sent later without you. Integrations The Settings tab where you connect accounts and switch channels on. Lead A person or business that could buy from you, on the Leads board. Measured / Not measured Measured: a real source answered. Not measured: no source did, so no figure is shown. Never a 0. See Measured and not measured. Missed A post whose time passed while it waited for approval. It is never sent late. Needs a connection Only a connected account can answer this. Needs you now What waits for you: plan tasks, drafts, replies (on Brand Analysis) or posts (on Campaigns). Not recorded It happened, but PULSE kept no record of it. Opportunity A public tender or request for proposals that matches what you sell. Partner A business, association, newsletter, creator or show you could work with. On Leads → Partners. Persona A kind of customer you talk to, taken from your check-up and your leads, never invented. See Personas. Plan Your plan (site fixes and the 30-day follow-up cycle) on Brand Analysis; or a campaign’s plan of phases and posts. Plan gate PULSE’s reviewer: it checks what PULSE proposes against the evidence before it is saved. Also called “PULSE’s reviewer” in the app. See The plan gate. Planned A post a campaign’s plan holds that is not written yet. Proposed by PULSE A campaign PULSE suggests from your check-up. It is read only until you accept it. Scheduled Approved, with a time to go out. Sent It really went out. Nothing reaches Sent by hand. Skill The way PULSE writes one kind of post (an Instagram Reel, a LinkedIn post …): instructions, then the checks. Step trail (“Its steps”) A post’s history: planned, drafted, approved, scheduled, then sent, withheld, failed or missed. Studio Where content is made (Make something new) and kept (My Library).
data.old-names#Old names: You may see It is now Site Audit, Overview, Research, Insights Brand Analysis and its pages Market Radar, Influencers Brand Analysis → What people are talking about, Leads → Partners Persona Profile, Intelligence Console, Customer 360 Removed from PULSE; those addresses open Leads Follow-up Leads → To do today, and Your plan on Brand Analysis Approval, Schedule, Publishing, Content board, Strategy, Content gaps, Roadmap Campaigns (the board and each campaign’s page) Creatives, Whitepapers, Shorts, Presentations, Courses, Reports Studio Automations Automate on each card Accounts, Data sources, System → Integrations Settings → Integrations Billing Settings → Subscription

data:
Settings → Integrations (/settings?tab=integrations) is one grid of cards, one per account or channel, in two sections:
Publish to: Instagram, YouTube, LinkedIn, Website, Website repository, Podcast, Audiobook, and Email (your mailbox). Measure & CRM: Google Analytics, Google Ads, Google Search Console, HubSpot, SAM.gov, and the Website form. Below the grid is Autopilot (see Autopilot and agencies).
This page is the owner’s side: what you click and what you get. Some connections first need your administrator to register PULSE with the platform (an app in Meta’s, Google’s or LinkedIn’s developer console). When that is missing, the card says so and names what the administrator must set. The administrator’s side is in Connections and Switches and arming order.
PULSE keeps every token and password encrypted, and never shows a pasted one again.
data.email#Email: Connect your own mailbox, so that Send on a lead’s email sends from your address: Connect Gmail, Connect Microsoft 365, or an SMTP server. With Gmail or Microsoft 365, PULSE also sees who replied. See Leads → Email.
data.google-analytics-and-google-ads#Google A:
These are connected with a key you create in Google Cloud and paste on the card:
Google Analytics: the JSON key of a service account with access to your GA4 property, and the numeric Property ID (GA4 Admin → Property Settings). Google Ads: the JSON key of a service account with domain-wide delegation, your Ads Customer ID, a Developer Token, optionally a Login Customer ID (manager account), and the user email to act as. Test Connection checks them. They fill the visits, page views, ad views, ad clicks and spend on Brand Analysis and in reports. If this is not something you do yourself, ask whoever manages your Google Cloud; the details are in Connections.
data.google-search-console#Google Search Cons:
Connect Search Console signs in with Google, read-only: PULSE never changes anything in Search Console. Then Choose the site PULSE reads; the one that matches the site you audited is marked. PULSE reads it once a day: the clicks, appearances, click rate and position of each search, for the last 28 days and the 28 before (Google’s figures run about two days behind).
The card says when it last read and up to which day, or why the last read failed. Read now, Change site and Disconnect are on it. If your Google account has no verified site, add your site at search.google.com/search-console first, then reconnect.
What it fills: Can people find you? on Brand Analysis, the Search clicks and Search impressions lines, and the demand behind content ideas and campaign plans (“people searched X; your site ranks 11”).
data.hubspot#HubSpot: Paste the access token of a HubSpot Private App (in HubSpot: Settings → Integrations → Private Apps) with the CRM contacts permissions. Then Sync from HubSpot on Leads imports your contacts, new leads PULSE finds are added to HubSpot, and your website form’s enquiries go there too.
data.instagram-youtube-and-linkedin#Instagram:
Connect opens the platform’s own sign-in in a new browser tab. Sign in, allow what PULSE asks for, then come back. (If nothing opens, allow pop-ups for PULSE.)
Once connected, the card shows:
Signed in, and when the sign-in ends. PULSE renews this sign-in before it ends where the platform allows it; otherwise it says Reconnect before that date. A failed renewal is shown with its date and reason. What each feature has: Publishing, Results, Comments and Direct messages, each allowed, needs a named permission, not checked, or not offered by that platform to apps (YouTube has no mentions and no direct messages for apps). Reconnect asks the platform again, for example to allow a permission you declined. Disconnect removes PULSE’s access at the platform where it can and deletes the stored sign-in; your settings for the account are kept. If your administrator has not set up sign-in for a platform, the card says … sign-in isn’t set up on this server and offers to paste a token instead. A pasted token works, but PULSE can neither check its permissions nor renew it, and the card says so.
Platform What you connect What PULSE does with it Instagram A professional (business or creator) Instagram account linked to a Facebook Page, through Facebook Login Publishes posts, carousels, Reels and Stories; reads results, comments, mentions and direct messages for Autopilot YouTube Your Google account and its YouTube channel Uploads Shorts; reads views, likes, comments and watch time LinkedIn Your LinkedIn member account Posts as you. Connect company pages (when your administrator has enabled it) lets you choose a company page you administer as the author instead
data.podcast-and-audiobook#Podcast and audiob: Nothing to connect: PULSE publishes these itself, in its own podcast feed that Spotify and Apple read. Turn them Active to use them.
data.samgov#SAM.gov: For US federal tenders on Opportunities: paste your SAM.gov public API key (on sam.gov: your profile, Account Details, API key). PULSE only reads opportunities with it.
data.website-form#Website form: Turns your site’s contact form into leads. See Website form.
data.website-repository#Website repository:
Fill in the Owner (your GitHub user or organization), the Repository name, the Base branch, and a Fine-grained access token: create it on GitHub under Settings → Developer settings → Fine-grained tokens, for this one repository only, with Contents and Pull requests set to Read and write. Then Connect and check. The card says Connected, or what is wrong: Missing permission, Token rejected, Base branch not found or GitHub unreachable. Check again re-checks it.
From then on, a fix the site score found can be proposed with Propose as pull request on the site-score report. PULSE writes the change on a new branch and opens a pull request for you to review and merge. PULSE never merges and never changes your base branch. Each fix shows its pull request’s state as last read from GitHub: Pull request open, Merged or Closed without merging, or No pull request needed, or Withheld by the plan gate when PULSE’s reviewer did not agree with the change.
Proposing needs an administrator account, and your administrator must have switched on publishing and site fixes on this PULSE. Until then the button is refused with the reason.
data.what-a-publish-to-card-tells-you#What a: Active: your switch. An Active channel gets PULSE’s daily drafts, is planned in your campaigns, and may publish. Turning it off stops all three. Save after changing it. A one-line status: Ready to publish, or Can’t publish: and the reason in plain words, for example Connect an account first., Publishing is switched off for this whole deployment. Posts are kept and marked held back., or Only this deployment’s named publishers can post here. Recent dispatches: what was posted, held back or failed, with the date.
data.your-website#Your website:
There are two cards, for two jobs:
Website publishes your approved blog articles to your site through GitHub. Paste a GitHub token that can push to your site’s repository. Which repository it publishes to is set by your administrator. Website repository is where PULSE proposes fixes to your site as pull requests. See below.

data:
Leads (/leads) is everyone outside your business in one page: the people who could buy from you, and, on the Partners canvas beside them, the partners, creators and shows you work with. A switch at the top moves between the two.
From top to bottom, the Leads canvas has: the HubSpot import (when HubSpot is connected), Who you’re looking for, To do today, the deal values, the replies to your emails, and the board.
data.calls#Calls:
Call on a lead opens the AI call. It is refused, with every reason listed, unless your administrator has turned AI calls on and the lead gave consent; see AI calls to leads. A lead can also be put on the do-not-call list from its AI call sheet.
Cold calling and cold email are regulated where you and your leads are: consent, calling hours, do-not-call lists, and unsubscribe rules. Check the rules that apply to you before you contact real people.
data.deal-value-and-won-revenue#Deal value an:
Moving a lead to Won asks what the deal was worth: an amount and a three-letter currency code (such as EUR). A lead cannot be marked won without a value. You can also give any open lead a value.
The strip above the board shows Won this month (per currency, never added across currencies) and the open value in New, Contacted and Qualified. Leads with no value are counted as “not valued”, never as 0. Deal values stay in PULSE; HubSpot receives contacts only.
data.email-from-your-own-mailbox#Email from y:
Connect your mailbox under Settings → Integrations → Email (Gmail, Microsoft 365 or SMTP). Then Send on an email draft sends the newest draft to the lead from your address, records it in the lead’s history, and moves a lead in New to Contacted. Send asks you to confirm first. It is not offered, and the sheet says why, when:
you are a viewer (sending needs an editor or admin); your administrator switched email sending off; no mailbox is connected, or it needs attention; you reached the daily limit. With Gmail or Microsoft 365, PULSE notices who replied and lists them under To do today. With SMTP it cannot read replies, and the page says so.
data.partners#Partners: The Partners canvas lists the partners your latest check-up found, with how to reach them and where they were found, then the partners, creators and shows you follow. Add a partner adds one by hand. Each partner has Partnership message, which drafts messages for you to copy and send yourself (PULSE does not send these), and its own automation. Stop following removes a partner; a later check-up that finds them again does not add them back.
data.the-board#The board:
Five columns: New, Contacted, Qualified, Won, Lost. Each lead is a card; tap it to open it. An open card shows the lead’s details, its next step, its History (the emails and AI calls to it) and its action row:
Draft writes a message for this lead: a Cold email, a Cold-call script or a LinkedIn DM. PULSE never sends a draft by itself. Send (on an email draft) sends it from your own mailbox. See Email. Call places an AI call, where your administrator has allowed them. Move changes the column. Add deal value / Edit deal value records what the deal is worth. Automate opens the lead’s own automation; see Automations.
data.to-do-today#To do today:
To do today lists, for each lead that is due, one next step in plain words, such as “send a follow-up email” or “place an AI call to book a meeting”, with Do it and Skip (moves it to tomorrow). A lead with no email or phone says so. It also lists:
leads who replied to an email you sent, with the first words of the reply and Answer; leads PULSE’s daily check says may go quiet, with its reason; your Weekly check-in: new followers, posts, engagement, leads and how satisfied you are this week, plus what worked and what didn’t. Your check-ins are what Your plan measures progress with, and Recalculate my plan from these check-ins re-plans the rest of the cycle; what Autopilot needs from you, for example an account it stopped posting to and why.
data.where-leads-come-from#Where leads come f: Source How Your check-ups A check-up finds leads for your niche and puts them in New, with the contact their page publishes and where they were found. Find Leads Finds businesses that publish a way to reach them and writes a first email, a call script and a LinkedIn message for each. It asks for a niche, a region, who buys from you, and competitors to leave out, filled in from your last check-up. 10 leads a run by default, at most 25. Add lead By hand. A lead needs at least a name, an email or a company. On a phone with no signal, it is saved and marked Queued until you are back online. Your website’s contact form Each enquiry becomes a lead in New. See Website form. HubSpot Sync from HubSpot imports your contacts. The bar says when it last synced and how many it read, or why it failed. PULSE shows HubSpot’s own lifecycle stage on a lead as it is, and does not score HubSpot leads itself. The board column is PULSE’s own.

data: Opportunities (/opportunities) finds public tenders and requests for proposals that need what you sell: a council website, an app, videos for a campaign. PULSE reads official open tender data every day and matches it on what your check-up found you sell. You decide, and you submit: PULSE reads and drafts, and never submits anything.
data.filters#Filters: Filters sets the countries (two-letter codes; empty means all), notices too close to their deadline to bother with, reminders before a deadline, the value range and its currency, public and private buyers, whether new matches show in the bell, and whether PULSE drafts a response for the best new matches by itself (this uses model time).
data.the-page#The page:
Due soon: what you are working on that closes within 14 days, soonest first. The counts: New this week, Matching, Closing within 14 days, In progress, Submitted, Won. Before the first look they read Not counted yet: PULSE has not looked. The board: Found → Interested → Preparing → Submitted → Won / Lost. Each card shows the buyer (public or private), the title, the value (Value not stated when the notice gives none), the deadline, Open the notice, and why it matched: the offering, words and codes it matched on. Its actions:
Draft response writes a response draft (Draft again to redo it). Move moves the card. Not for us sets it aside, with your reason. Automate opens its own automation.
data.the-response-draft#The response draft: Draft response (not sent) lays out: Why you, What the notice asks, what is Answered, what is Not covered: add it yourself, Documents to prepare, Before you send, the deadline and how to submit. Copy draft copies it as plain text. Check it, complete it, send it yourself, then move the card to Submitted. A draft PULSE’s checks or reviewer refused says Not drafted and why.
data.where-pulse-looks#Where PULSE looks:
Source Needs EU tenders (TED) Nothing UK Find a Tender · UK Contracts Finder Nothing Brazil public purchases (PNCP) Nothing CanadaBuys Nothing Requests for proposals on the web Nothing US federal (SAM.gov) Your own SAM.gov public API key, pasted on the SAM.gov card in Settings → Integrations Where PULSE looked says, for each source, what the last look got: notices read, nothing new, could not be read (with the reason), or not connected (with what to do). These are four different answers, never an empty list.
PULSE looks once a day. Look now looks straight away. If your administrator switched the daily look off, the page says so and Look now still works.

data: PULSE shows a result only when something measured it: your own records (what PULSE did), a platform that reported it (Instagram, LinkedIn, YouTube), or an account you connected (Google Analytics, Google Ads, Search Console). Anything else reads Not measured, never 0 and never an estimate. See Measured and not measured.
data.reports#Reports:
Make a report in Studio → Long reads and audio → Report:
Timeframe, for example Last 30 Days or Q1 2025. Left empty, it is the last 30 days. A period that reaches past today ends today. Highlight metrics (optional), separated by commas. File to download: PDF Document or CSV / Spreadsheet Data. PULSE first reads your measured records for the period (metrics, the results of your posts, won revenue) and writes the figures itself. The model is given only those figures, to write the reading around them, and any sentence naming a figure that is not in your records is removed. Each source is one of three things: measured (its figures in a table), not measured, or unreadable with the reason. A metric you asked to highlight that nothing measured is listed as not measured. If nothing at all was measured, the model is not asked to write.
The PDF has a title page with your account and the period, the reading, the measured figures as tables, and what was not measured. It is laid out in your language (English, Spanish, French or Portuguese) with that language’s number format, with every accented letter, curly quote, dash and the euro sign drawn as written. The finished file is also kept in My Library.
Guides, study guides, mind maps, timelines and comparison tables made in Studio are PDFs too.
